title: The Most Entangled States Of Four And Seven Qubits
authors: Antony Lewis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pure states of four and seven qubits cannot be maximally entangled across every balanced bipartition; we determine how entangled they can be on average. For four qubits we prove the conjecture of Higuchi and Sudbery: the mean von Neumann entropy of the three [MATH] cuts is at most [MATH] bits, with equality exactly on the local-unitary orbits of their state [MATH] and its complex conjugate. For seven qubits the mean purity of the 35 balanced [MATH] cuts is at least [MATH] and their mean entropy is at most [MATH] bits, each with a unique optimiser up to local unitaries and qubit permutations. The two optimisers are distinct members of one icosahedral family, so minimum purity and maximum entropy select different states. The proofs bound moments of the marginal spectra by positive identities on several copies of the state, some of them spin flipped, and bound the entropy by a polynomial in those moments. The four-qubit maximum has an analytic proof; the seven-qubit proofs, and some of the four-qubit refinements below, are computer-assisted, with exact arithmetic and rigorous error bounds. We also prove the Gour--Wallach conjecture for R\'enyi entropies of all orders, with the maximiser changing from [MATH] to cluster states at [MATH], and obtain sharp Tsallis bounds, mixed-state bounds and quantitative stability.
tldr: Determines the maximal average entanglement across balanced bipartitions for four and seven qubit pure states, proving the Higuchi-Sudbery and Gour-Wallach conjectures and providing sharp bounds on entropy and purity.
motivation: Understanding how entanglement is distributed among subsystems in multipartite quantum states is fundamental, and prior conjectures about optimal entanglement measures lacked rigorous proof.
method: Bounds moments of marginal spectra using positive identities on several copies of the state, some spin-flipped, and then bounds entropy via a polynomial in those moments; proofs are analytic for four qubits and computer-assisted with exact arithmetic for seven qubits.
result: For four qubits, the mean von Neumann entropy of the three 2-2 cuts is at most a specific value with equality on local-unitary orbits of two states; for seven qubits, the mean purity of the 35 balanced cuts is at least a certain value and the mean entropy is at most a certain value, each with a unique optimizer up to local unitaries and permutations; also proves the Gour-Wallach conjecture for Rényi entropies of all orders and obtains sharp Tsallis bounds.
conclusion: Provides rigorous characterization of maximally entangled states for four and seven qubits, advancing entanglement theory and entropy inequalities with implications for multipartite entanglement quantification.

title: Norm Bounds On Sums Of Positive Operators With Applications To Monogamy Games And Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Marco Tomamichel Salman Beigi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bounding the acceptance probabilities of quantum measurements is a recurring task in quantum information theory. We prove a general inequality for such norms, valid for arbitrary finite families of positive semidefinite operators and averaging distributions. We give two applications of our operator-norm inequality. First, we determine the sharp robustness threshold for the parallel BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game. For error thresholds [MATH], when the two players may make at most [MATH] and [MATH] errors, respectively, the optimal winning probability decays exponentially if [MATH], tends to one exponentially fast under the reverse strict inequality, and remains bounded away from zero on the boundary. Second, we establish the achievability of every asymptotic key rate [MATH] for one-sided device-independent BB84 quantum key distribution with tolerated bit-error rate [MATH] and asymptotically optimal reconciliation, where [MATH] is the binary entropy function. Alice's measurements are trusted, while Bob may perform an arbitrary joint measurement depending on the entire basis string, subject to the protocol's receipt and isolation requirements. This recovers the usual BB84 rate in this model.

motivation: Bounding acceptance probabilities of quantum measurements is central to monogamy games and device-independent cryptography, but existing tools often lack sharp, general bounds for averaged positive operators.

title: From Claws To Conferences: Device-Independent Key Agreement Beyond Non-Signaling
authors: Suvradip Chakraborty
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) allows a group of users to establish a common secret key without trusting the internal operation of their quantum devices. Existing DI-CKA protocols derive their security from multipartite Bell tests and therefore require the device components not to communicate during each round. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first DI-CKA protocol that removes this non-signaling assumption: all interfaces and their mutual communication are treated as one untrusted device, which only has to be quantum polynomial-time while the protocol runs. Assuming that the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem is hard for quantum algorithms with quantum advice during the execution, we prove finite-size security against coherent attacks, in which the device may keep quantum memory and correlate and adapt its behavior across rounds. For two parties the protocol is a computational DI-QKD protocol with an explicit finite-size proof against coherent attacks. Technically, we lift the claw state underlying the classical-verifier test of Brakerski et al.\ (FOCS 2018) to multipartite entanglement, obtaining a . %that is prepared with one coherent claw-free function evaluation and [MATH] CNOT gates. We then introduce the , a multiparty generalization of the adaptive hardcore bit of Brakerski et al.\ and show that it follows from the original property by a tight reduction. Combined with Jordan's lemma, an entropic uncertainty relation, and entropy accumulation, this certifies smooth min-entropy of the key against an external quantum adversary. Our protocol achieves : LWE needs to hold only during the execution, because the final key is statistically secure and its secrecy persists even if LWE is broken after the protocol ends.

motivation: Existing DI-CKA protocols rely on multipartite Bell tests and require device components not to communicate during each round, which is a strong operational assumption. The work aims to remove this non-signaling assumption while retaining device-independent security.

result: Assuming LWE hardness for quantum algorithms with quantum advice during execution, the authors prove finite-size security against coherent attacks where the device may retain quantum memory and adapt across rounds. For two parties, this yields a computational DI-QKD protocol with an explicit finite-size security proof.
conclusion: The protocol achieves security whose final key remains statistically secure even if LWE is broken after the protocol ends, enabling DI-CKA beyond the non-signaling assumption.

title: Dynamically Modulated Light-matter Interactions For Ancilla-tolerant Bosonic Control
authors: Aniket Maiti, John W. O. Garmon, Daniel K. Weiss, Takahiro Tsunoda, Yao Lu, Steven M. Girvin, Robert J. Schoelkopf
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong light-matter interactions are central to state-of-the-art quantum technologies, spanning platforms as diverse as Rydberg atoms, trapped ions, and superconducting circuits. In superconducting circuits, the strong dispersive coupling between microwave photons (light) and ancillary qubits (matter) has enabled universal bosonic control and quantum error correction. However, this always-on dispersive interaction propagates errors from the ancillary qubits to the bosonic systems both while idling and when performing operations, introducing a trade-off between control strength and fidelity. We break this trade-off by introducing a parametrically activated hybridization between the bosonic modes and ancilla qubits, keeping both elements decoupled when not active. When activated, this hybridization mediates a dynamic light-matter coupling with non-trivial engineered symmetries, permitting resilience to ancilla decay and dephasing. This dynamic coupling functions as a new control primitive that offers a route to bosonic processors whose performance is set by the oscillator, rather than the ancilla.

abstract: ArXiv:2611.05541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Defining entropy of a quantum channel has become a challenge with potential candidates recently reported in literature. title: Multipartite Entanglement Swapping With Homodyne And Single Photon Detection
authors: Josephine Dias Tarek Assaf
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Establishing multipartite entanglement across lossy optical networks remains a central challenge for distributed quantum information processing. Here, we consider a non-Gaussian continuous-variable entanglement-swapping protocol combining a symmetric discrete Fourier transform (DFT) interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection. In the ideal limit, single-photon heralding generates a [MATH]-class state across remote modes, with Fourier symmetry rendering all single-click outcomes equivalent up to local phase corrections. We find that conditional pairwise entanglement can exceed that of conventional Gaussian homodyne swapping in weak-to-moderate squeezing and lossy regimes, remaining nonzero beyond the channel-loss thresholds at which Gaussian pairwise entanglement vanishes. These results demonstrate that combining non-Gaussian measurements with symmetric interferometric mixing can improve both the resilience and operational efficiency of multipartite entanglement distribution in lossy quantum networks.

title: Spectral Measures And Sharpness Of Quantum Speed Limits
authors: Ivica Smoli\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum speed limits bound the time required for a given state to evolve into a given subspace of the Hilbert space under specific energy constraints. We prove that for several standard orthogonalization time bounds, the unique spectral measure associated with the initial vector that saturates the bound is a sum of two Dirac measures. Furthermore, we constrain the families of spectral measures that come arbitrarily close to these bounds and construct examples with measures which are purely absolutely continuous and purely singular continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. As a complementary perspective, we discuss the geometric intuition behind quantum speed limits provided by the numerical range of the evolution operator.

result: For several standard bounds, the unique saturating spectral measure is a sum of two Dirac measures; families of near-saturating measures can be purely absolutely continuous or purely singular continuous, and the numerical range provides geometric intuition.
conclusion: The work sharpens the characterization of quantum speed limits by identifying extremal spectral measures and showing that near-saturation is achievable by broad classes of measures.

title: Toward A Quantum Information Foundation For Neutron Scattering
authors: Michael J. Landry, Yongqiang Cheng, Daniel Pajerowski, Joshua J. Turner, Mingda Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutron scattering is a central probe of quantum materials, yet what quantum information can, in principle, be extracted from a scattering experiment remains unclear. Here we formulate neutron scattering as a quantum measurement, with the scattering amplitudes acting as Kraus operators on the material state. This provides a unified description of conventional intensity, coherent scattering, interferometric measurements, and entanglement witnesses, including those based on quantum Fisher information. title: Classical Records And Bell Correlations In A Dynamically Formed Quantum Body
authors: Hao Sun Xinxin Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Competing quantum contacts can create a boundary that was absent from the specification of a subsystem. We construct approximately isolated bodies from bare field vacuum and zero-centred contact packets. A binding contribution with vanishing mean energy density nevertheless changes a bounded formation signal by order one at the same clock. On the formed material spins and their original memories, coarse collective records precede an all-outcome Bell violation. The field evolves dynamically, with the finite bath, residual boundary interaction, failed records and preparation costs retained. The result connects dynamical subsystem formation, classical collective records and microscopic nonlocality, with polynomial resources in the stated preparation and measurement class.

title: Bounded Decoding Complexity In Transversal Circuits With Magic State Injection
authors: Giacomo Giudice Lukas M. Sieberer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize the complexity of space-time correlated decoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures that implement Clifford gates transversally and realize non-Clifford gates via magic state injection. In this approach, decoding graphs for logical measurements are constructed by backpropagating measurement operators through the circuit, which causes them to grow with circuit volume. However, the decoding volume can be substantially reduced by decoding measurements sequentially, committing corrections, and excluding syndrome data that have already been processed for earlier measurements. For random circuits, we find that the resulting decoding volume associated with mid-circuit measurements approaches a stationary average that is determined by the density of magic state injections. Large decoding instances are exponentially suppressed. We further find that the decoding complexity is remarkably insensitive to different choices of measurement products to be decoded, and that the same qualitative behavior persists across different circuit connectivities and Clifford gate ensembles. These results suggest that scalable space-time correlated decoding of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum algorithms is achievable since the magic states that make transversal architectures universal also keep them decodable.

method: The authors construct decoding graphs by backpropagating measurement operators through the circuit and study sequential decoding with committed corrections and exclusion of already-processed syndrome data, analyzing random circuits across connectivities and gate ensembles.
result: The decoding volume approaches a stationary average set by the magic-state injection density, large decoding instances are exponentially suppressed, and the complexity is insensitive to measurement-product choices and circuit details.

title: Efficiently Tracking Errors And Outcomes In Universal Quantum Circuits
authors: Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente Thomas R. Scruby
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a method for efficient simulation of error propagation and decoding in universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under stochastic Pauli noise, requiring only that the circuit has a high fault distance and that all logical non-Clifford operations are implemented by physical T, CS and CCZ gates. This is achieved using modified Pauli frame-based error tracking in which the frame contains no logical information. Decoding success is identified by verifying that the Pauli frame is still logically trivial after decoding. Using the results of Ref. [1] and the observation that the distribution of non-logical measurement outcomes in the circuit is independent of the logical state, we show that we can accurately sample all detector outcomes. Our approach can also simulate circuits containing adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements, provided these measurements have a known outcome distribution. This applies to the majority of adaptive operations such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement. Our method only detects decoding failures and so is consistent with complexity-theoretic expectations as it cannot be used to sample from the noiseless outcome distribution of the logical circuit.

motivation: Simulating full fault-tolerant universal circuits with non-Clifford gates and decoding is computationally demanding, and existing Pauli-frame techniques struggle to handle logical outcomes and adaptive operations without full simulation.

result: The approach accurately samples all detector outcomes and can handle adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements with known outcome distributions, such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient practical tool for tracking errors and decoding failures in universal fault-tolerant circuits, though it only detects decoding failures and cannot sample the noiseless logical outcome distribution, consistent with complexity-theoretic bounds.

title: The Structure Of Shared Classical Facts In Quantum Systems
authors: Jie Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Perfectly matching local outcomes need not constitute a nondisturbing shared classical record. For finite-dimensional multipartite states, we prove that nontrivial exact records are equivalent to a spectrum sharing structure with a unique finest decomposition into locally distinguishable sectors, where entanglement may persist. For a fixed complete pointer, exact sharing is equivalent to strong quantum Darwinism together with global nondisturbance, while spectrum broadcast structure additionally requires conditional independence. Arbitrarily weak full-rank admixtures eliminate exact sharing, but two-sided distance bounds quantify robustness through disturbance and disagreement, while information bounds connect accurate local readouts to observer consensus.

result: Spectrum broadcast structure requires additional conditional independence; arbitrarily weak full-rank admixtures destroy exact sharing, while distance and information bounds quantify robustness via disturbance, disagreement, and observer consensus.
conclusion: The analysis provides a structural and robustness framework for shared classical facts in quantum systems, distinguishing exact objectivity from approximate consensus under noise.

title: SPAM-robust Learnability Of Quantum Dynamics
authors: Zitai Xu, Guoding Liu, Senrui Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate characterization of quantum dynamics is essential for the calibration and control of quantum devices. Unknown state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors, however, introduce gauge ambiguities that limit what can be learned. A central question is therefore which properties are learnable despite SPAM errors, and whether physical structure in the dynamics can restrict these ambiguities and expand the set of learnable properties. In this work, we address both questions within a unified framework for quantum channels and continuous-time evolution. First, for general quantum channels and Lindbladian dynamics, we use the cycle structure of a generalized pattern-transfer graph to fully characterize all learnable parameter combinations and show achievability by constructing explicit SPAM-robust learning protocols, establishing a baseline where continuous gauge freedom prevents many individual parameters from being identified. Second, we show that coherent structure drastically restricts this gauge ambiguity, reducing continuous gauge freedom to discrete or even trivial choices. This restriction manifests across both discrete- and continuous-time settings, including purely Hamiltonian evolution, noisy quantum channels close to a target unitary, and Lindbladian dynamics close to a target Hamiltonian. In particular, when the dynamics preserves or remains close to a coherent Hamiltonian form, all coherent coefficients and broad classes of dissipative error parameters become individually learnable. These results establish a systematic route to exploiting physical structure for SPAM-robust characterization, providing a foundation for the reliable calibration and control of quantum devices.
tldr: The paper characterizes which parameters of quantum channels and Lindbladian dynamics remain learnable under unknown SPAM errors and shows that coherent Hamiltonian structure can reduce gauge ambiguities and restore individual learnability.
motivation: Accurate characterization and calibration of quantum devices are limited by SPAM-induced gauge ambiguities, so it is important to determine which dynamical properties are learnable despite these errors and whether physical structure can improve identifiability.
method: The authors introduce a generalized pattern-transfer graph and use its cycle structure to classify all learnable parameter combinations for general quantum channels and Lindbladian dynamics, then analyze how coherent Hamiltonian structure restricts gauge freedom in discrete- and continuous-time settings.
result: For general channels and Lindbladians, continuous gauge freedom prevents many individual parameters from being identified, but near or purely Hamiltonian dynamics reduce this ambiguity to discrete or trivial choices, making coherent coefficients and broad classes of dissipative parameters individually learnable.
conclusion: Physical structure can be systematically exploited to achieve SPAM-robust characterization, providing a foundation for reliable calibration and control of quantum devices.

title: A Study Of Fluctuation Growths Of Observables In Open Quantum Systems
authors: Newshaw Bahreyni, Paul M. Alsing, Carlo Cafaro, Walid Redjem, Christian Corda
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rate at which quantum fluctuations of observables can change provides a useful characterization of the dynamical behavior of quantum systems. For closed quantum systems undergoing unitary evolution, previous work has established a general upper bound on the growth rate of the uncertainty of an observable in terms of the standard deviation of its dynamical velocity. This result is closely related to quantum acceleration limits and provides a compact constraint on fluctuation growth. In this work, we will briefly review the closed system results and extend this perspective to open quantum systems, where the state evolves nonunitarily as a consequence of interactions with an environment. The central result is an upper bound on the rate of growth of the uncertainty of an observable that remains valid for general density-matrix dynamics. We develop two complementary derivations. The first introduces a Hermitian pseudo-Hamiltonian describing the local unitary evolution of the eigenvectors of the density matrix. The second, and more general, derivation proceeds directly from the density-matrix derivative and therefore does not require knowledge of the generator of the dynamics. Both approaches lead to the same fluctuation-growth bound. An important practical advantage is that the bound can be evaluated from the observable, the state, and its time derivative without requiring reconstruction of the complete dynamical generator.
tldr: The paper extends bounds on the growth rate of quantum fluctuations of observables from closed unitary systems to general open quantum systems with nonunitary density-matrix dynamics.
motivation: Rate of change of quantum fluctuations characterizes dynamics, and closed-system bounds linked to quantum acceleration limits exist; the authors ask whether an analogous constraint holds when the state evolves nonunitarily due to an environment.
method: Two complementary derivations: (i) a Hermitian pseudo-Hamiltonian describing local unitary evolution of the density matrix eigenvectors, and (ii) a direct derivation from the density-matrix derivative that avoids reconstructing the dynamical generator.
result: Both approaches yield the same upper bound on the rate of growth of an observable's uncertainty, valid for general density-matrix dynamics and computable from the observable, state and its time derivative alone.
conclusion: Fluctuation-growth bounds survive in open-system settings and offer a practical, generator-free diagnostic of nonunitary quantum dynamics, generalizing quantum acceleration/speed-limit-type constraints.

title: Raychaudhuri-Ehlers Kinematics On Quantum State-Space: Caustics And Extrinsic Quantum Geometry
authors: Neellohit Karmakar, Suraj S. Hegde, Aryan Bhatia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum mechanics is inherently geometric in that the pure states form a curved complex manifold and the Schr\"odinger evolution defines a Hamiltonian flow on this space. Geometry identifies constraints on flows on quantum state-space that hold independently of their microscopic realization. We uncover such universal behavior in families of geodesic paths on the quantum state-space using the Raychaudhuri-Ehlers equations. We show that the complex structure leads to tidal anisotropy in the curvature, and for Hilbert space dimension [MATH], complete point-emitted geodesic bundles necessarily develop shear and undergo direction-selective focusing at finite distance. We give these geometric results an information-theoretic interpretation in terms of fidelity susceptibility and quantum Fisher information. For ground-state manifolds constrained by physical parameters, we resolve the tidal curvature into Berry-curvature-dependent ambient tides and contributions from extrinsic bending within the full ambient state space. We further relate extrinsic bending to variations in the unitary generator of motion along intrinsic geodesics. We present exact many-body geometric results for the transverse-field XY spin chain. The product structure of the ground state leads to an exact cancellation of the ambient tide, including its Berry-curvature enhancement, by extrinsic curvature contributions. At the zero-field Ising point, we obtain exact results at finite size and show that the shear source for anisotropy-directed motion is entirely extrinsic relative to the full many-body state-space. For the metric in the thermodynamic limit, the geodesic families exhibit repeated [MATH] fold catastrophes inside the ferromagnetic phase. Our framework thus separates universal state-space effects from those of physical restrictions and exposes their consequences in a paradigmatic many-body system.
tldr: The paper applies Raychaudhuri-Ehlers kinematics to quantum state-space, showing universal geodesic focusing and caustic formation with information-theoretic interpretations via fidelity susceptibility and quantum Fisher information.
motivation: The authors aim to uncover universal geometric constraints on Hamiltonian flows in quantum state-space that are independent of microscopic realization, and to connect them to quantum information measures.
method: They analyze geodesic bundles on the complex projective Hilbert space using Raychaudhuri-Ehlers equations, decompose curvature into intrinsic and extrinsic contributions, and evaluate exact results for the transverse-field XY spin chain.
result: For Hilbert-space dimension greater than two, geodesic bundles develop shear and direction-selective focusing; ambient tidal effects can cancel against extrinsic bending in the XY chain, and repeated fold catastrophes appear in the thermodynamic-limit metric.
conclusion: The framework separates universal state-space geometry from physically constrained ground-state manifolds and exposes geometric consequences in a paradigmatic many-body system, with potential relevance to quantum information geometry.

title: Tensor-network Simulation Of Strongly Coupled Multi-fluxonium Circuits
authors: Christian Hensel, Andr\'es N. C\'aliz, Pau Torrente, Mar\'ia Hita-P\'erez, Arnau Riera
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing a superconducting quantum processor rests on predicting the low-lying spectrum of its coupled circuit. The Hilbert-space dimension of the circuit's lumped-element model grows exponentially with the number of circuit nodes. The usual methods split the circuit into subsystems, but that split is hard to choose when the elements are strongly coupled. We present a tensor-network method that chooses no subsystems and whose memory and run time per solve are set by the number of modes and two truncations, the Fock cutoff of each normal mode and the bond dimension of a matrix product state (MPS), not by the Hilbert-space dimension. From the capacitance matrix, the inverse-inductance matrix and the junction list alone, the linear circuit is diagonalized into normal modes. Each junction cosine is then a sum of two products of single-mode operators, so the complete lumped-element Hamiltonian is a matrix product operator (MPO) of small bond dimension with one site per mode, solved by the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). The normal modes make the method generic, and the tensor network makes it affordable. For two fluxonia joined by a tunable coupler, the method agrees with exact diagonalization of the same truncated space to within 1 MHz. Our circuit of three fluxonia joined by two couplers has 11 normal modes and a truncated space of [MATH] states, out of reach of exact diagonalization in dense or sparse storage. At a bond dimension of 32, its lowest eight levels are converged to within 1 MHz in both truncations, and each state is stored in a small fraction of the numbers a dense vector needs. One solve at that bond dimension takes 81 min and 1.3 GB of memory on one CPU node.
tldr: The paper introduces a tensor-network method for simulating the low-lying spectrum of strongly coupled multi-fluxonium superconducting circuits using normal-mode decomposition and DMRG.
motivation: Designing superconducting quantum processors requires predicting the spectrum of coupled circuits, but exact diagonalization becomes intractable as the number of nodes grows, and subsystem splitting is difficult for strongly coupled elements.
method: The linear circuit is diagonalized into normal modes from the capacitance and inverse-inductance matrices; each junction cosine is expressed as a sum of products of single-mode operators, yielding an MPO Hamiltonian solved with DMRG.
result: For two fluxonia with a tunable coupler, the method agrees with exact diagonalization within 1 MHz; for three fluxonia and two couplers with 11 modes, the lowest eight levels converge at bond dimension 32 within 1 MHz, using 81 min and 1.3 GB on one CPU node.
conclusion: The normal-mode tensor-network approach provides an affordable and generic simulation tool for strongly coupled superconducting qubit circuits such as multi-fluxonium processors.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper presents a tensor-network method for computing the low-lying spectrum of superconducting quantum processor circuits without partitioning the circuit into subsystems. The method leverages the quadratic nature of the linear part of the circuit to diagonalize it into normal modes, using only the capacitance matrix, inverse-inductance matrix, and junction list. Each Josephson junction cosine is then expressed as a sum of two products of single-mode operators, making the full Hamiltonian a matrix product operator (MPO) with one site per mode and small bond dimension. The density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) is then applied to solve for the low-energy eigenstates. The approach is demonstrated on a system of two fluxonia joined by a tunable coupler, where it agrees with exact diagonalization to within 1 MHz. For a more complex circuit of three fluxonia and two couplers with 11 normal modes and a truncated space of 10^9 states, the method converges the lowest eight levels to within 1 MHz using a bond dimension of 32, with each state stored compactly. A single solve takes 81 minutes and 1.3 GB of memory on one CPU node.

Validation against exact diagonalization for a two-fluxonium-plus-coupler system, showing agreement within 1 MHz.

Scaling to a three-fluxonium-plus-two-coupler circuit with 11 modes and a truncated space of 10^9 states, achieving convergence of the lowest eight levels to within 1 MHz at bond dimension 32, with each state stored in a small fraction of a dense vector's size.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The method begins by diagonalizing the linear part of the circuit (capacitance and inverse-inductance matrices) to obtain normal modes. This transformation is exact for the quadratic part and yields a set of independent harmonic oscillators. Each Josephson junction contributes a cosine term that, when expressed in terms of normal-mode coordinates, becomes a sum of two products of single-mode operators (since cos(φ) = (e^{iφ} + e^{-iφ})/2 and φ is a linear combination of mode operators). This structure allows the full Hamiltonian to be written as an MPO with one site per mode and a bond dimension that depends on the number of junctions but remains small. The MPO is then used with DMRG to find the low-lying eigenstates. The truncation parameters are the Fock cutoff per mode and the bond dimension of the MPS. The authors emphasize that the method requires no manual partitioning and is thus applicable to strongly coupled systems where choosing subsystems is difficult. The approach is generic because it only requires the circuit's linear parameters and junction list.
deep_read.results_analysis: For the two-fluxonium-plus-coupler system, the method agrees with exact diagonalization of the same truncated space to within 1 MHz, validating the MPO construction and DMRG implementation. For the three-fluxonium-plus-two-coupler circuit with 11 normal modes, the truncated space has 10^9 states, which is beyond exact diagonalization with dense or sparse storage. At a bond dimension of 32, the lowest eight levels are converged to within 1 MHz in both truncations (Fock cutoff and bond dimension). Each state is stored in a small fraction of the numbers a dense vector would require, demonstrating the memory efficiency. A single solve at that bond dimension takes 81 minutes and 1.3 GB of memory on one CPU node, which is feasible for practical use. These results show that the method can handle circuits with many modes and strong coupling, where traditional partitioning would be challenging.

The approach is demonstrated only for circuits with a relatively small number of modes (up to 11); scaling to larger numbers of modes may require larger bond dimensions and could become computationally expensive.
The paper does not discuss the treatment of non-linear elements beyond Josephson junctions (e.g., higher-order terms) or the inclusion of dissipation, which may be relevant for realistic processors.

It addresses a key challenge in quantum information processing: predicting the low-lying spectrum of coupled circuits with many degrees of freedom. The tensor-network approach, combining normal-mode diagonalization with DMRG, offers a powerful numerical tool for analyzing strongly coupled superconducting circuits, which are central to quantum computing hardware. Overall, this is a high-quality contribution that bridges tensor-network techniques and circuit quantum electrodynamics.

title: Zero Noise Extrapolation Of Transport Coefficients
authors: Hansveer Singh, Pieter Claeys, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Anushya Chandran
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: NISQ devices routinely estimate properties of the noiseless system from measurements at varying noise strengths [MATH]. These zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) schemes fail to estimate transport coefficients of conserved quantities when the noise violates the associated conservation laws. We show how to extrapolate measurements in noisy, one-dimensional, non-integrable spin chains to obtain the spin transport coefficients governing linear response in the zero-noise limit. As the wavevector of the Fourier mode of a conserved quantity goes to zero, its decay rate vanishes. The coefficient of the leading momentum dependence defines a transport coefficient in the noiseless system, and an analogous effective coefficient in the noisy one. Naive ZNE implicitly assumes that this effective coefficient is analytic in [MATH] as [MATH]. Our main result is that universal non-linear corrections to hydrodynamics can produce non-analytic dependence on [MATH]. In particular, we argue that the effective spin diffusion coefficient of a dissipative Heisenberg chain and the effective subdiffusion coefficient of a dipole-conserving fracton approach their noiseless value as [MATH]. We benchmark these analytical predictions numerically.
tldr: The paper analyzes zero-noise extrapolation for transport coefficients in noisy one-dimensional spin chains and shows that hydrodynamic nonlinearities can produce non-analytic noise dependence, requiring modified extrapolation.
motivation: NISQ devices rely on zero-noise extrapolation to estimate noiseless properties, but such schemes can fail for transport coefficients when noise violates conservation laws. This work aims to understand and correct the extrapolation of transport coefficients in noisy many-body quantum systems.
method: The authors study Fourier modes of conserved quantities in noisy, non-integrable spin chains, derive effective diffusion and subdiffusion coefficients in the presence of dissipation, and benchmark analytical predictions numerically.
result: They find that universal nonlinear corrections to hydrodynamics can make the effective transport coefficients depend non-analytically on noise strength, with examples including spin diffusion in a dissipative Heisenberg chain and subdiffusion in a dipole-conserving fracton model.
conclusion: Naive zero-noise extrapolation can be unreliable for transport coefficients; accounting for non-analytic hydrodynamic corrections is necessary to extract reliable zero-noise transport properties from NISQ measurements.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses a critical issue in zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) for quantum simulation on NISQ devices: when noise violates conservation laws, standard ZNE fails to correctly estimate transport coefficients. The authors focus on one-dimensional non-integrable spin chains and show that the effective transport coefficients extracted from noisy measurements have non-analytic dependence on the noise strength γ as γ→0. Specifically, they argue that for a dissipative Heisenberg chain, the effective spin diffusion coefficient approaches its noiseless value as γ^{1/2}, and similarly for the subdiffusion coefficient in a dipole-conserving fracton model. This non-analyticity arises from universal non-linear corrections to hydrodynamics. The authors support their analytical predictions with numerical benchmarks, demonstrating that naive polynomial extrapolation in γ would fail, and propose a modified extrapolation scheme that accounts for the γ^{1/2} behavior. The work has implications for extracting transport properties from noisy quantum devices and highlights the interplay between noise, conservation laws, and hydrodynamics.

They consider one-dimensional non-integrable spin chains with conserved quantities, such as energy or spin, and introduce noise that violates the associated conservation laws (e.g., dephasing or particle loss). title: Quantum Error Correcting Codes From Quiver Moduli: Grassmannians, Cyclic Monodromy, And Argyle Collision Divisors
authors: Evan Sundbo Steven Rayan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on aspects of a recent diagrammatic field-theory programme for quantum error correction put forward by the first-named author (arXiv:2607.08911), we construct exact finite-dimensional codes from twisted cyclic and argyle quiver moduli on the projective line. title: Symmetry-guided Algorithms For Variational Quantum Optimization
authors: Eunjin In, Kristina D. Launey, Darin C. Mumma, James A. Sauls
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert--Schmidt asymmetry (\(\AHS\)), which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit \(S\)-wave \(p+{}^3\) two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, \(\AHS\)-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.

motivation: Hardware-efficient ansatzes can break symmetries and explore irrelevant sectors, reducing optimization accuracy and ground-state fidelity.
method: The authors define an asymmetry measure AHS based on group action and use it as an objective to guide variational optimization without enforcing symmetry in the preparation circuit, demonstrated for SU(2) singlet targets.
result: AHS-guided optimization improves energy accuracy and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with larger fidelity gains in up to 12-spin collective models.
conclusion: Group-action-derived asymmetry provides a Hamiltonian-independent objective useful for reliable variational quantum optimization in symmetry sectors.

title: Sympathetic Cooling Of Ionic Fullerenes With Ultracold Atoms To Millikelvin Temperatures

abstract: ArXiv:2611.05815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooling complex molecular ions to millikelvin temperatures remains a major challenge because their intricate internal structures prevent laser cooling. Here, we propose to use an ultracold gas of Cd atoms to efficiently cool C[MATH] ions to average kinetic energies of approximately 20 mK, following an initial precooling stage with He buffer gas. Our approach is based on full molecular dynamics simulations using accurate ion-atom interaction potentials derived from high-level electronic structure methods. Furthermore, using a Monte Carlo approach, we predict the formation of C[MATH] Coulomb crystals supported solely by collisions with the buffer gas. The probability of reaching these cold states shows a pronounced dependence on the number of trapped ions, revealing the competition between neutral-atom cooling and many-ion dynamics in radio-frequency traps.

title: Essential Unitarity For Higher-Order Quantum Computation (Extended Abstract)
authors: Radha Jagadeesan Samson Abramsky (university College London)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a boundary-centric semantic framework for higher-order quantum computation, building on the Kelly-Laplaza description of compact closure and Abramsky's execution account. In the semantic carrier Perm(C), morphisms are complex-linear combinations of polarized boundary linkings, composed by execution. Finite-family addresses provide coherent control over finite-level quantum registers (qudits) while retaining the multiplicative boundary structure. We identify essential unitarity, a boundary condition extending ordinary unitarity to higher-order interfaces. On positive qudit registers it coincides with ordinary matrix unitarity; at higher order it expresses preservation of information across the full polarized boundary. We define a unit-free coherent quantum core generated bymultiplicative wiring, unitary gates on positive qudit registers, and contextual coherent control, and prove that every one of its morphisms is essentially unitary. The framework realizes an applied coherent quantum switch and the unitary stages of equal-ratio one-slot supermap dilations with explicit memory. Complete proofs appear in the full version of this paper.
tldr: The paper develops a categorical semantics for higher-order quantum computation and introduces essential unitarity as a boundary condition extending ordinary unitarity to higher-order quantum interfaces.
motivation: Higher-order quantum computation requires semantic foundations that account for coherent control, supermaps, and preservation of information across interfaces beyond ordinary unitary gates.
method: It builds on compact closure and Abramsky's execution account, using morphisms in Perm(C) as complex-linear combinations of polarized boundary linkings and finite-family addresses for coherent control over qudit registers.
result: Essential unitarity coincides with matrix unitarity on positive qudit registers and is preserved by all morphisms in a coherent quantum core generated by wiring, unitary gates, and contextual coherent control; the framework realizes a coherent quantum switch and unitary stages of supermap dilations.
conclusion: The work provides a boundary-centric semantic account of higher-order quantum computation where unitarity is extended to higher-order interfaces, supporting coherent control and supermap constructions.

title: Krylov Meets Fock: Complementary Lenses On Quantum Dynamics
authors: Dimitrios Patramanis Giuseppe Di Giulio
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum dynamics in Krylov space can be represented by a particle hopping on a chain whose sites are the Krylov basis vectors. The goal of this work is to extend this idea to the Fock basis, which in turn allows the description of a generic dynamics in terms of a more general, possibly higher-dimensional lattice. This construction has been dubbed the Fock state lattice (FSL), since its sites are identified with Fock states. To analyze the dynamics on the FSL we introduce various measures of the spread of a state, comparing them among themselves and with their Krylov counterparts. We apply our analysis to two models of light-matter interaction studied in quantum optics: the multi-mode Jaynes-Cummings and the Dicke models. We find that, whenever the FSL is not a chain, the corresponding dynamics provides insights complementary to the Krylov space analysis and, in some instances, greater analytical control. For example, we obtain analytical results for the FSL spread measures of the Dicke model in the thermodynamic limit and determine that their scaling in time detects the superradiant phase transition.
tldr: The paper extends Krylov-space dynamics to a Fock-state lattice and compares spread measures in multi-mode Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models.
motivation: Krylov-space dynamics gives a chain representation of quantum evolution, but the authors argue that the Fock basis can provide a more general, possibly higher-dimensional lattice picture with complementary insights.
method: They introduce the Fock state lattice (FSL) and several spread measures, then apply the framework to the multi-mode Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models, including analytical results in the thermodynamic limit.
result: When the FSL is not a chain, its spread measures offer complementary analytical control; for the Dicke model, their time scaling detects the superradiant phase transition.
conclusion: The FSL provides a useful complementary lens to Krylov-space analysis for quantum dynamics, particularly in light-matter models with non-chain Fock lattices.

title: Noise-Induced Topology In Chiral Quantum Walks
authors: Alexandre Chaduteau, Derek K. K. Lee, Frank Schindler, Abhinav Prem
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noise typically destroys quantum coherence and washes out transport phenomena that rely on interference. Chiral quantum walks are a case in point: a particle hopping on a lattice threaded by a magnetic flux can spread asymmetrically due to interference between paths, an asymmetry that noise is expected to erase. Remarkably, we find that the most ubiquitous noise -- random fluctuations of on-site energies (dephasing) -- instead renders this asymmetry topologically robust. The density profile develops a skewness that grows in time while its center stays fixed, and in a finite chain the late-time relaxation modes pile up at one edge: a skin effect lacking the drift of conventional non-Hermitian skin effects. With multiple sites per unit cell, the dephasing strength alone can cause a topological phase transition, reversing the asymmetry. On a flux ladder with noisy rung hopping, the noise causes a drift of rung coherences, a quantum ratchet with no classical counterpart. Underlying these effects, the noise-averaged dynamics is an interacting (generically non-integrable) Lindbladian that remains analytically tractable. The modes governing late-time relaxation are bound states of the noise-induced interaction and form a band with a point gap, absent both without noise and under postselection, whose winding number fixes the direction of the asymmetry. These effects are within reach of several experimental platforms, including synthetic lattices, superconducting qubits, and optical lattices.
tldr: The paper shows that dephasing noise can induce topologically robust chiral transport and a non-Hermitian-like skin effect in chiral quantum walks via a tractable interacting Lindbladian.
motivation: Chiral quantum walks rely on interference, so noise is usually expected to destroy their asymmetric transport; the authors ask whether dephasing can instead create robust topological effects.
method: They analyze noise-averaged quantum walk dynamics, map it to an interacting Lindbladian, and use late-time relaxation modes, point-gap topology, and winding numbers to characterize the induced asymmetry.
result: Dephasing produces a growing skewness with a fixed center, edge-piling relaxation modes, dephasing-driven topological transitions, and a quantum ratchet effect in a flux ladder.
conclusion: Noise-induced topology in open quantum walks provides a counterintuitive route to robust chiral transport, with possible implementations in synthetic lattices, superconducting qubits, and optical lattices.

title: Fermionic Porter-Thomas Statistics And Their Emergence In Random Matchgate Circuits
authors: Guglielmo Lami
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For Haar-random quantum states, measurement probabilities follow the universal Porter--Thomas distribution. This implies anticoncentration, i.e.\ the spreading of probability over exponentially many outcomes, a key property underlying random-circuit-sampling experiments. We derive the exact analogue of the Porter--Thomas law for random fermionic Gaussian states, both with and without particle-number conservation. We also consider Clifford Gaussian states, for which the problem maps onto a simple model of arcs and loops. For large systems the probabilities become log-normally distributed, with moments growing polynomially in system size. Free-fermion states thus anticoncentrate only up to polynomial factors. We then show how this fermionic Porter--Thomas law emerges in random one-dimensional brickwork matchgate circuits. A simple single-arc approximation accurately describes the full distribution of probabilities, revealing an early diffusive regime followed by a slow relaxation on times scaling as the square of the system size. We rigorously prove that depths growing almost quadratically with system size are required for the collision probability to converge. Finally, we show that ideal free-fermion sampling yields large linear cross-entropy scores, and propose a log-based benchmark with an exact fermionic normalization.
tldr: The paper derives fermionic analogues of Porter-Thomas statistics for random Gaussian and Clifford Gaussian states and shows how these statistics emerge in random matchgate circuits.
motivation: Porter-Thomas statistics and anticoncentration underlie random-circuit-sampling experiments, but the fermionic Gaussian analogue and its emergence in matchgate circuits were not fully characterized.
method: The author computes exact measurement-probability distributions for Haar-random fermionic Gaussian states with and without particle-number conservation, analyzes Clifford Gaussian states via an arcs-and-loops model, and studies random 1D brickwork matchgate circuits.
result: Fermionic probabilities become log-normal with polynomially growing moments, so free-fermion states anticoncentrate only up to polynomial factors; in matchgate circuits a single-arc approximation describes the distribution and almost quadratic depth is required for collision-probability convergence.
conclusion: Ideal free-fermion sampling can produce large linear cross-entropy scores, motivating a log-based benchmark with exact fermionic normalization.

title: Algorithmic Wave-Particle Duality: Pathfinding In Welded Trees Is Hard
authors: Joseph Carolan, Andrew M. Childs, Matthew Coudron, Amin Shiraz Gilani, David Miloschewsky, Supartha Podder
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the welded trees problem, an algorithm navigates a randomly labeled graph formed from two binary trees joined at their leaves through a "weld" of connecting edges. A quantum walk can navigate from root to root exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, recording its path destroys the constructive interference responsible for the speedup, leaving open whether some quantum algorithm can efficiently find a path between the roots. We prove that, for trees of height [MATH], the quantum query complexity of finding a path between the roots with constant probability is [MATH]. This establishes an algorithmic wave-particle duality, adapting the double-slit experiment to the high-complexity regime: interference between many paths lets a quantum algorithm reach the exit efficiently, but finding a single path (the algorithmic analog of the route of a particle) requires exponentially many queries. Furthermore, the bound is tight, matching the cost of a quantum algorithm that finds collisions between paths from each root to the weld. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle to track the information about the graph that an algorithm retains and forgets. We show that the compressed database remains close to a space of states that do not record a path between the roots by bounding the error introduced by each compressed oracle query.
tldr: The paper proves an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding a path between the roots in the welded-trees problem, establishing an algorithmic form of wave-particle duality.
motivation: Quantum walks solve the welded-trees navigation problem exponentially faster than classical algorithms, but it was unclear whether a quantum algorithm can also output an explicit path without destroying the interference enabling the speedup.
method: The authors use the compressed permutation oracle to track the information an algorithm retains or forgets about the graph, bounding the error introduced by each query to show the compressed database remains close to states that do not record a root-to-root path.
result: For trees of height n, they prove the quantum query complexity of finding a path between the roots with constant probability is exponential, and the bound is tight via an algorithm that finds collisions between paths from each root to the weld.
conclusion: The work establishes a high-complexity analogue of the double-slit experiment: many interfering paths allow efficient root-to-root navigation, but extracting a single path requires exponentially many queries.

title: Classical Training Of Conditional Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time Born Machines
authors: Oriol Ball\'o-Gimbernat, Emiliano Tolotti, Laia Domingo, Fernando Vilari\~no, Adan Garriga
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) Born machines are attractive quantum generative models, as certain IQP circuit families are conjectured to be hard to sample, yet they can be trained classically. Previously proposed conditional IQP Born machines make the parameters of the diagonal layer condition dependent. We introduce conditional IQP Born machines, in which the condition is encoded in the input state and a single IQP unitary is shared across conditions. Efficient sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation for the reference state entering the diagonal layer suffice to obtain unbiased classical estimates of a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective and its gradients. We show that input conditioning can represent conditional families that no diagonally conditioned IQP model with the same number of qubits can reproduce. For the sixteen-qubit Curie-Weiss spin model, a single conditional model captures the magnetization transition at held-out temperatures. Its mean total variation distance is six times lower than that of diagonal conditioning under the same protocol and comparable to that of classical generative models with up to seven times as many parameters. We also train conditional models classically with up to 2048 qubits, which reproduce the mean squared magnetization of the target away from the crossover. These results extend classically trained IQP Born machines to conditional generation.
tldr: The paper introduces conditional IQP Born machines where conditioning is encoded in the input state, enabling classical training and sampling for conditional generative modeling.
motivation: IQP Born machines are promising quantum generative models that can be trained classically, but existing conditional variants use diagonal-layer conditioning, which may limit representational power.
method: The authors encode the condition in the input state and share a single IQP unitary across conditions; they derive unbiased classical estimates of a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective and its gradients using efficient sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation.
result: Input conditioning is shown to represent conditional families inaccessible to diagonal conditioning with the same qubit count; on a 16-qubit Curie-Weiss model, a single conditional model captures the magnetization transition with mean total variation distance six times lower than diagonal conditioning, and models up to 2048 qubits reproduce mean squared magnetization away from the crossover.
conclusion: The work extends classically trained IQP Born machines to conditional generation, demonstrating representational and practical advantages over prior diagonal conditioning approaches.

title: Fano's Inequality And Channel Capacity In The Individual-Sequence Regime
authors: Neri Merhav
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an individual-sequence analogue of Fano's inequality, replacing entropy by Lempel--Ziv (LZ) complexity and probability of error by empirical error frequency. In the setting considered, an arbitrary encoder maps a message to a channel input sequence [MATH], the channel maps the input to an output [MATH] in a completely arbitrary manner, and a block finite-state decoder produces an estimate of the channel input from the output. The individual-sequence Fano inequality lower-bounds the empirical symbol-error frequency in terms of the LZ complexity of the channel input conditioned on the channel output. This leads to a channel coding converse: reliable communication at a given rate is possible only if that rate does not exceed the individual-sequence LZ channel capacity, defined as the LZ mutual information maximized over channel inputs and minimized (worst-case) over a noise set. We also prove a matching achievability theorem for the class of channels, in which the channel output at each time [MATH] is [MATH], [MATH] being a `noise' variable, and [MATH] is a bijection for every fixed [MATH]. This class includes group-additive channels [MATH] studied by Feder and coworkers. For such a channel, any rate below the LZ capacity is achievable with vanishing per-message error frequency, simultaneously for every [MATH] in a given noise set [MATH], provided [MATH] is closed under block permutations; this condition is satisfied by any noise set that depends on [MATH] only via its type class with respect to such blocks. The achievability uses a universal decoder that requires no knowledge of the channel and no feedback.
tldr: The paper derives an individual-sequence Fano inequality using Lempel-Ziv complexity and applies it to characterize channel capacity in a worst-case, individual-sequence regime.
motivation: Classical Fano's inequality is fundamentally an average-case entropy bound; the author seeks an individual-sequence analogue that avoids probabilistic entropy assumptions and yields channel-coding converses for arbitrary encoders and finite-state decoders.
method: The paper replaces Shannon entropy with Lempel-Ziv complexity and error probability with empirical error frequency, proving a lower bound on symbol-error frequency in terms of conditional LZ complexity. It then defines an LZ mutual-information channel capacity and proves converse and matching achievability for a class of bijective-noise channels.
result: Reliable communication at rate R is possible only if R does not exceed the individual-sequence LZ channel capacity, defined as worst-case LZ mutual information over a noise set; for bijective-noise channels including group-additive channels, any rate below capacity is achievable with vanishing per-message error frequency using a universal decoder.
conclusion: The work extends Fano's inequality and channel capacity to an individual-sequence, complexity-based setting, providing worst-case coding theorems for finite-state decoders without channel knowledge or feedback.

title: Quantum Resource Trade-offs Of Mixed Sparse Single And Double Factorization For Qubitization-based Phase Estimation
authors: Troy Losey, Jacob Z. Williams, Avanish Mishra, Jian-Xin Zhu, Yu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a mixed block encoding of quantum-chemistry Hamiltonians for quantum phase estimation (QPE) on fault-tolerant quantum computers. Following a Cholesky decomposition of the electron repulsion integral tensor, we assign each Cholesky tensor to either a double-factorization (DF) branch or a sparse-single-factorization (SPSF) branch. This freedom permits a trade-off between reducing the block-encoding normalization factor [MATH] with DF and reducing the coefficient data loaded through quantum read-only memory (QROM) with SPSF. Resource estimates across molecular benchmarks show, however, that the mixed circuit does not generally reduce the Toffoli count relative to the less expensive pure circuit. The main obstacles are the overhead of loading substantial data through separate branch-specific QROMs and the limited benefit of mixing when the pure DF and SPSF circuits have dissimilar costs. Modest savings occur only in restricted parameter regimes, most clearly when logical-qubit requirements are included in the cost metric. These results identify the circuit-level conditions that a useful mixed block encoding must satisfy.
tldr: The paper studies a mixed block-encoding strategy combining double factorization and sparse single factorization for qubitization-based quantum phase estimation of quantum-chemistry Hamiltonians, finding limited Toffoli-count savings.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum chemistry simulations require reducing resource costs in block encodings for QPE, and mixing DF and SPSF branches could trade normalization against QROM data loading.
method: After Cholesky decomposition of the electron repulsion integral tensor, each Cholesky tensor is assigned to either a double-factorization or sparse-single-factorization branch, and circuit resource estimates are compared across molecular benchmarks.
result: The mixed circuit generally does not reduce Toffoli count relative to the cheaper pure circuit because of separate branch-specific QROM overhead and dissimilar branch costs; modest savings appear only in restricted regimes, especially when logical-qubit cost is included.
conclusion: The work identifies circuit-level conditions that a useful mixed block encoding must satisfy, but the proposed mixing is not broadly advantageous for reducing phase-estimation costs.

title: Trinetra.Q: Statistical And Behavioral Detection Of Attacks On The Quantum-Error-Correction Layer And Classical Control Stack Of Quantum Computing Systems
authors: Garrv Sipani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most quantum-computer security work targets physical-layer attacks on qubits, while two surfaces remain inadequately defended: the quantum-error-correction (QEC) syndrome-and-decoder pipeline, and the classical control and software stack that runs it. Tampering on these surfaces can corrupt a computation while the physical error rate appears normal, and can stay within a single-circuit integrity tolerance. We present Trinetra.Q, a detection layer of cooperating detectors, each monitoring a statistical or behavioral property of quantum-domain data against an envelope calibrated from honest operation, and raising an indication only on a statistically significant deviation. The detectors cover (A) QEC integrity over per-stabilizer firing rates, syndrome defect-count, and repeated-syndrome rate; (B) decoder confidence over the margin between minimum-weight error explanations in distinct logical classes; (C) behavioral output divergence, flagging crosstalk-class and novel attacks by their effect on a victim's output relative to a matched control; (D) control-stack tampering via known-answer canary circuits, built to be indistinguishable to a resident implant, with a cross-job consistency statistic; and (E) compilation/execution integrity. Each gates on significance, so honest operation raises no alarm. We evaluate in faithful simulation and on three production IBM Heron processors, and bound the physical attack surface with a systematic negative map: most physical-layer attacks return statistically null, the exception an implemented, measured within-job feed-forward covert-channel primitive. Every detector is also evaluated against an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of it. To our knowledge this is the first unified statistical-and-behavioral detection layer for the QEC layer and classical control stack of a quantum computing system, demonstrated on production hardware.
tldr: Trinetra.Q is a statistical and behavioral detection layer that monitors the QEC syndrome/decoder pipeline and the classical control/software stack of quantum computers to flag integrity attacks.
motivation: Most quantum-computer security research focuses on physical-layer attacks on qubits, leaving the QEC syndrome-and-decoder pipeline and the classical control stack undefended, where tampering can corrupt computations while physical error rates appear normal.
method: The authors deploy cooperating detectors that monitor per-stabilizer firing rates, syndrome defect counts, decoder confidence margins, output divergence against matched controls, known-answer canary circuits, and compilation/execution integrity, each gated on statistical significance; they evaluate in simulation and on three IBM Heron processors against an adaptive attacker.
result: Honest operation raises no alarms while tampering on the studied surfaces is detected, and a systematic negative map shows most physical-layer attacks yield statistically null signals, with one measured within-job feed-forward covert-channel primitive as an exception.
conclusion: The work claims the first unified statistical-and-behavioral detection layer for the QEC and classical control stack of a quantum computer, demonstrated on production hardware, though its contribution is systems/security engineering rather than quantum information theory.

title: Efficient Training Of A 128-modes 3d Continuously Coupled Photonic Chip Via Limited Quantum Resources
authors: Denis Stanev, Simone Di Micco, Francesco Hoch, Taira Giordani, Nicol\`o Spagnolo, Marco Gardina, Andrea Crespi, Francesco Ceccarelli, Roberto Osellame, Fabio Sciarrino
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated photonics provides a promising route towards the development of large-scale, stable and low-loss quantum hardware. Existing implementations of universal quantum photonic chips generally rely on architectures consisting of localised interactions between the modes that can be programmed with known algorithms to implement specific operations. Recent advances have shown that interferometers based on 3D continuously coupled waveguide arrays may allow to significantly scale up the number of modes with reduced overhead. However, for this class of devices, optimal strategies to set the controllable parameters and obtain the desired transformation have not been demonstrated generally. In this work, we report the use of a machine learning algorithm driven by quantum data to program the operation of a reconfigurable three-dimensional continuously coupled photonic device comprising 128 modes. We show experimentally the capability of reaching a target unitary matrix, among those achievable by the device, through a limited number of one- and two-photon measurements. Our results demonstrate that this approach results to be effective in the presence of noise and with a limited amount of resources, also allowing to partially compensate imperfections in the experimental setup. This method can thus represent a viable route towards programming large scale integrated photonic devices, unlocking the possibility of controlling photonic systems for which an analytical decomposition is not trivial.
tldr: A machine-learning algorithm is used to program a 128-mode 3D continuously coupled photonic chip via limited one- and two-photon measurements to approximate a target unitary.
motivation: Large-scale programmable photonic hardware is promising for quantum information processing, but optimal strategies for setting 3D continuously coupled devices without analytical decompositions are lacking.
method: The authors experimentally drive a quantum-data-based machine learning algorithm to configure a reconfigurable 128-mode 3D photonic device, using a limited number of one- and two-photon measurements to reach an achievable target unitary.
result: The approach successfully programs the device, remains effective under noise, partially compensates experimental imperfections, and works with limited quantum resources.
conclusion: This method offers a practical route to controlling large-scale integrated photonic systems where analytical decomposition is intractable.

title: Hardware Demonstration Of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced Mcmc For Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
authors: Keisuke Fujii Yuya Kawamata
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with [MATH] binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with [MATH], where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately [MATH] and [MATH] times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a hardware implementation of neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced MCMC for constrained Boltzmann sampling on an IBM Quantum processor.
motivation: Neural-surrogated QeMCMC can accelerate Boltzmann sampling using QAOA samples, but optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem in a divide-and-conquer scheme is costly, motivating a hardware-efficient implementation.
method: The authors implement neural-surrogated QeMCMC on an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor and test it on binary-variable systems, extending the demonstration to a system with more than one thousand variables via divide-and-conquer.
result: They observe faster autocorrelation decay for suitable subproblem sizes, but also identify challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks; the per-step autocorrelation decay rate exceeds that of global and local Kawasaki dynamics by approximately specified factors.
conclusion: The work shows that quantum-hardware-generated samples can accelerate autocorrelation decay in large constrained Boltzmann sampling, while highlighting limitations in neural-surrogate scalability.

title: Pauli Gadget Synthesis For Gatesets With Arbitrary Even Arity Clifford Gates
authors: Arianne Meijer - van de Griend Leo Becker (university Of Helsinki)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an algorithm that can synthesize circuits to gate sets consisting of a 2n-arity Clifford gate and arbitrary single qubit rotations. To do this, we represent the circuit as a sequence of Pauli gadgets and jointly synthesize them by placing the multi-qubit Clifford in the synthesized circuit and pushing its adjoint through the remaining gadgets such that some qubits are disconnected from some gadgets. The pushed gadgets are collected in a Clifford tableau, which is decomposed afterwards. With the help of our algorithm we run experiments where we synthesize circuits to varying sizes of target multi-qubit gates. These experiments indicate that increases in gate size can lead to smaller output circuits, and that different connectivity constraints have meaningful differences in how higher arity gates effect the circuit sized.
tldr: The paper introduces an algorithm that synthesizes quantum circuits into gatesets composed of a single 2n-arity Clifford gate plus arbitrary single-qubit rotations, by jointly synthesizing Pauli gadgets and pushing Clifford adjoints through them.
motivation: Fault-tolerant architectures increasingly offer high-arity Clifford gates (e.g., from lattice surgery or multi-qubit encodings), but existing synthesis tools assume CNOT-based or fixed gatesets, leaving circuit compilation for such gatesets unaddressed.
method: Circuits are represented as sequences of Pauli gadgets; the multi-qubit Clifford is inserted and its adjoint pushed through remaining gadgets to disconnect qubits, with the accumulated gadgets collected in a Clifford tableau that is subsequently decomposed.
result: Experiments across varying target multi-qubit gate sizes show that larger-arity gates can yield smaller output circuits, and that different connectivity constraints produce meaningfully different scaling of circuit size with arity.
conclusion: The approach offers a practical compilation route for even-arity Clifford gatesets, suggesting higher-arity hardware primitives may reduce circuit cost, though benefits depend strongly on connectivity.

title: Neuromorphic Camera For Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition And Tracking In Free Space Optical Communication
authors: Francesco Nardo, Nigitha Selvaraj, Klaus Schertler, Peter Kr\"otz, Ricardo Barrios, Sebastian Houben, Sebastian Randel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.
tldr: The paper evaluates event-based (neuromorphic) vision sensors and tracking algorithms for simultaneous multi-beacon pointing, acquisition, and tracking in free-space optical communication links.
motivation: PAT systems in FSOC need both wide field of view and low jitter, but conventional frame-based cameras suffer from latency, limited frame rate, and motion blur, motivating asynchronous event-based sensing.
method: A neuromorphic event sensor recording brightness changes with microsecond resolution is used, and several event-based tracking algorithms operating directly on the asynchronous event stream are compared on an experimental dataset emulating dynamic HAP/UAV network conditions.
result: Tracking accuracy and processing latency of the candidate algorithms are benchmarked across varying signal-to-background conditions, showing event-based sensing as a viable low-latency alternative for multi-target acquisition and tracking.
conclusion: Event-based vision is a promising route for PAT in aerial free-space optical links, though the work is an applied hardware/algorithm comparison without quantum information content.

title: Time-resolved Infrared Spectroscopy With Entangled Photons And Visible-light Detection
authors: Jasleen Kaur, Yu Mukai, Ryo Okamoto, Shigeki Takeuchi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved infrared (TR-IR) spectroscopy reveals molecular structural changes and charge-carrier dynamics on their intrinsic timescales, in photosynthesis, catalysis and optoelectronic materials, but requires complex sources of ultrashort infrared pulses, cryogenically cooled detectors to overcome thermal background, and intense probes that can perturb the sample. Quantum infrared spectroscopy avoids these constraints: harnessing quantum interference between the generation processes of frequency-entangled photon pairs, it reads out the infrared response of a sample by detecting only the visible partner photon, for which efficient detectors exist.
