To date, it has been limited to steady-state measurements. Here we demonstrate its ultrafast, time-resolved form with a picosecond visible pump pulse and a silicon detector. Each visible pulse generates photon pairs within a picosecond window; the infrared photon of a pair probes the excited sample at a set delay after excitation, and the transient response is read out from the count rate of its visible partner. We resolve picosecond carrier dynamics in a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror near 1529 nm with a picowatt-level probe, unaffected by thermal background and by sample IR photoluminescence 50 times stronger than the probe. The approach is applicable to the mid-infrared, fingerprint region, where infrared detection is hardest, and to the terahertz region.
tldr: The paper demonstrates time-resolved infrared spectroscopy using frequency-entangled photon pairs and visible-light detection, enabling ultrafast carrier dynamics measurements without infrared detectors.
motivation: Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy is powerful but requires complex ultrashort infrared sources, cryogenic detectors, and intense probes that can perturb samples. Quantum infrared spectroscopy using entangled photons avoids these constraints but had only been shown in steady-state measurements.
method: The authors use a picosecond visible pump pulse and a silicon detector to detect the visible partner of frequency-entangled photon pairs, whose infrared partner probes the excited sample at a controlled delay. The transient infrared response is read out from the visible photon count rate.
result: They resolve picosecond carrier dynamics in a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror near 1529 nm using a picowatt-level probe, unaffected by thermal background and by sample infrared photoluminescence 50 times stronger than the probe.
conclusion: This work extends quantum infrared spectroscopy to the time domain and is applicable to the mid-infrared fingerprint and terahertz regions where infrared detection is most difficult.

title: A Liquid Vapor Phase Transition In Quantum Statistical Mechanics
authors: Francesco Baffioni, Tobias Kuna, Immacolata Merola, Errico Presutti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a liquid vapor phase transition for a quantum system of particles in the continuum. The system is the quantum version with Boltzmann statistics of the point particles model introduced in by Lebowitz, Mazel and Presutti.
tldr: The paper rigorously proves a liquid-vapor phase transition for a continuum quantum system of particles with Boltzmann statistics.
motivation: The authors aim to extend a classical point-particle model of Lebowitz, Mazel, and Presutti to the quantum setting and establish the existence of a liquid-vapor phase transition there.
method: They analyze a quantum statistical-mechanical model of particles in the continuum using rigorous mathematical techniques, treating the quantum version with Boltzmann statistics.
result: They prove that the quantum continuum particle system exhibits a liquid-vapor phase transition.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous quantum analogue of the classical Lebowitz-Mazel-Presutti phase-transition result, contributing to mathematical quantum statistical mechanics rather than quantum information or information thermodynamics.

title: Dynamical Signatures Of Selective Gap Closing In Multi-Dimensional Monotone Quasiperiodic Operators
authors: Roman Shterenberg Leonid Parnovski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We translate the spectral gap-closing criterion for multi-dimensional monotone quasiperiodic Schr\"odinger operators into a concrete dynamical protocol and verify it by large-scale numerics. For a non-principal label we construct a sampling function whose leading eigenfunction weight at the origin vanishes; a local bump then drives the residual weight through zero. The height of a weighted oscillatory time average of the origin-to-localization-center correlator exhibits a deep minimum precisely at the closing, while the site-control label remains featureless and orders of magnitude larger. The signature is robust and maps directly onto superconducting-circuit and photonic platforms.
tldr: The paper translates a spectral gap-closing criterion for multi-dimensional monotone quasiperiodic Schrödinger operators into a dynamical protocol and verifies it numerically.
motivation: Spectral gap-closing criteria for quasiperiodic operators are abstract; the authors aim to provide a concrete dynamical signature that can be measured in physical platforms.
method: For a non-principal label, they construct a sampling function with vanishing leading eigenfunction weight at the origin, apply a local bump to drive residual weight through zero, and use a weighted oscillatory time average of the origin-to-localization-center correlator.
result: The correlator exhibits a deep minimum exactly at gap closing, while the site-control label remains featureless and orders of magnitude larger, yielding a robust dynamical signature.
conclusion: The proposed protocol maps directly onto superconducting-circuit and photonic platforms, offering an experimentally accessible way to detect selective gap closing in quasiperiodic systems.

title: Quantum Advantage In Sensing And Imaging Through Coherent Nuisance Suppression
authors: Maxim Sirotin, Aleksandr Mokeev, Ishaan Kannan, Julian C. Christou, Jayadev Rajagopal, Babak Saif, Mikhail D. Lukin, Johannes Borregaard
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many sensing and imaging problems must contend with unknown nuisance parameters such as aberrations, background fields, and drift, and the cost of removing these noise sources can dominate the sample budget. In contrast to classical receivers, a quantum receiver can processes samples jointly to directly access observables in which common nuisance is suppressed. We introduce a relational Fourier sampling algorithm for optimal, source-independent imaging with a programmable quantum camera, which uses quantum pixels and a quantum computer to capture and process photon states. We demonstrate its relevance for general astronomical imaging as well as super-resolution and transient-object tracking through drifting atmospheric turbulence. A quantum camera that resolves an optical wavefront across [MATH] spatial modes using [MATH] receiving qubits, with a full-rank and strongly-correlated nuisance over those modes, can yield an exponential sample-complexity reduction of [MATH]. For typical seeing conditions at leading ground-based observatories, we predict more than three orders of magnitude fewer photons to resolve point-source positions using only 15 processing qubits and a depth-9 circuit. Our work identifies coherent nuisance suppression as a novel mechanism for provable quantum advantage with direct relevance to many sensing tasks.
tldr: The paper proposes a relational Fourier sampling algorithm using a programmable quantum camera to suppress coherent nuisance parameters and achieve exponential sample-complexity reductions in sensing and imaging.
motivation: Sensing and imaging tasks are often limited by unknown nuisance parameters such as aberrations, background fields, and atmospheric drift, whose removal can dominate the sample budget.
method: The authors introduce a relational Fourier sampling algorithm in which a quantum receiver processes photon states jointly across spatial modes using quantum pixels and a quantum computer, targeting observables where common nuisance is suppressed.
result: For a quantum camera resolving an optical wavefront across many spatial modes with strongly correlated nuisance, they predict an exponential reduction in sample complexity, with over three orders of magnitude fewer photons needed for point-source localization under typical observatory seeing conditions.
conclusion: Coherent nuisance suppression is identified as a mechanism for provable quantum advantage in sensing and imaging, with applications to astronomical imaging, super-resolution, and transient-object tracking through turbulence.

title: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization Via Density Matrix Renormalization Group
authors: Yuto Sugimoto, Tomonori Shirakawa, Yukio Kawashima, Toshinari Itoko, Seiji Yunoki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce SqDMRG, which combines sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). SqDMRG expands the sampled determinant space into a product of fragment spaces constructed from the samples, and solves the Hamiltonian in this product space using DMRG. We demonstrate the method on benzene pentamer and decamer clusters using classical reference samples, and on the pentamer using quantum samples obtained from the IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor ibm phoenix. It achieves sub-kcal/mol accuracy with far fewer configurations than direct diagonalization.
tldr: SqDMRG combines sample-based quantum diagonalization with DMRG to solve molecular Hamiltonians efficiently in a fragment product space.
motivation: Quantum chemistry calculations on near-term quantum processors require reducing the exponential cost of diagonalizing sampled determinant spaces while retaining accuracy.
method: The authors expand sampled determinant spaces into products of fragment spaces and solve the Hamiltonian in this product space using DMRG, tested with classical samples for benzene pentamer/decamer and quantum samples from ibm_phoenix.
result: SqDMRG reaches sub-kcal/mol accuracy with far fewer configurations than direct diagonalization on benzene clusters.
conclusion: The method provides a scalable hybrid quantum-classical route for molecular electronic structure, but it is specialized to quantum chemistry rather than the targeted quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-system directions.

title: Rough-to-frozen Transition In Non-integrable Dimer Models
authors: Alessandro Giuliani, Vieri Mastropietro, Bruno Renzi, Fabio Toninelli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The transition from rough to frozen phases in models of random surfaces is expected to be governed by the Pokrovsky-Talapov law, which predicts a [MATH]-type singularity of the macroscopic height profile (limit shape), as the distance [MATH] from the frozen phase (facet) is sent to zero. This has been proved so far only in exactly solvable cases, notably the classical, determinantal, 2D dimer model. In this paper we prove the validity of the Pokrovsky-Talapov law for a non-integrable 2D dimer model on the hexagonal lattice, whose Gibbs weight depends upon a weak plaquette interaction among dimers. Our proof is based on a multiscale analysis (constructive fermionic Renormalization Group), which allows us to identify two different regimes with distinct scaling properties and to explain the universality of the Pokrovsky-Talapov exponent [MATH], in contrast with the interaction-dependent critical exponents characterizing the rough phase. The first regime, corresponding to smaller distances, is characterized by an effective quadratic dispersion relation, while the second comes with an effective linear dispersion relation, typical of Luttinger liquid behavior. As a byproduct of our construction, we control the scaling limit of the interacting dimer model uniformly in the distance from the frozen phase.
tldr: The authors rigorously prove the Pokrovsky-Talapov law governing the rough-to-frozen (facet) transition for a non-integrable, weakly interacting 2D dimer model on the hexagonal lattice.
motivation: The Pokrovsky-Talapov behaviour of limit shapes near facets has previously been established only in exactly solvable models such as the classical determinantal dimer model; whether it survives non-integrable perturbations, and why its exponent is universal, was open.
method: A multiscale analysis in the form of a constructive fermionic renormalization group is applied to the interacting dimer model, identifying two scaling regimes with effective quadratic and linear (Luttinger-liquid-like) dispersion relations.
result: The Pokrovsky-Talapov square-root singularity of the height profile is proven, with the exponent shown to be universal while the rough-phase critical exponents depend on the interaction; the scaling limit is controlled uniformly in the distance from the frozen phase.
conclusion: The work extends limit-shape universality beyond integrable dimer models and clarifies the mechanism behind the stability of the Pokrovsky-Talapov exponent under interactions.

title: On The Most Informative Boolean Function Under Noise
authors: Mert Saglam Dimiter Kramer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a uniform random bit string and [MATH] be obtained by flipping each bit of [MATH] independently with probability [MATH]. Let [MATH] be a random bit obtained as a function of [MATH]. We show that [MATH] for all [MATH], which resolves a conjecture posed by Courtade and Kumar in 2013.
tldr: The paper proves the Courtade-Kumar conjecture that dictatorship maximizes mutual information for Boolean functions of uniformly random bits observed through a binary symmetric channel.
motivation: It addresses a fundamental classical information-theoretic question: which Boolean function retains the most information about a noisy observation of its input bits.
method: The authors provide an analytical proof resolving a conjecture posed by Courtade and Kumar in 2013.
result: They show the conjectured mutual-information inequality holds for all noise parameters, establishing dictatorship as the most informative Boolean function under independent bit-flip noise.
conclusion: This settles a longstanding conjecture in classical information theory, confirming the optimality of dictatorship for the binary symmetric channel setting.

title: Topological Localization In Unentangled Random Braids
authors: Daniil Fedotov, Pieter Hendrik Willem van der Hoek, Sergei Nechaev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2015, P. Serna, G. Bunin, and A. Nahum numerically investigated fluctuations in a bunch of unentangled random threads. They showed that fluctuations of an individual thread in a braid are qualitatively different from those of a thread embedded in a medium of fixed parallel lines. In particular, Serna et al. observed a logarithmic increase in the average transverse span, [MATH], of a thread with polymer length, [MATH]. This behavior highlights the collective nature of topological interactions, in which each polymer fluctuates and constrains the motion of the others. Studying this problem both numerically and analytically, we propose the following interpretation: the logarithmic regime is transient, and sufficiently long polymers exhibit topological localization, where [MATH] approaches a finite limit at [MATH]. Unlike localization induced by quenched external disorder, this phenomenon arises solely from collective topological constraints. We study braids within a locally free approximation and support the localization by analytical investigation of Brownian bridges on the asymptotic Cayley graph of a locally free group. We further conjecture that topologically induced localization emerges as a phase transition: for a small number of threads, [MATH], the span, [MATH], grows algebraically, with the usual scaling [MATH] at [MATH]; by contrast, for sufficiently large [MATH], each thread in a long braid ([MATH]) asymptotically localizes, approaching [MATH].
tldr: Numerical and analytical study of unentangled random polymer braids showing that the transverse span of a thread saturates (topological localization) rather than growing logarithmically, with a conjectured transition between algebraic growth and localization as the number of threads increases.
motivation: Serna, Bunin and Nahum observed a logarithmic growth of transverse span with polymer length in unentangled random braids, unlike the fixed-parallel-lines case; the authors aim to reinterpret this regime as transient and to explain the underlying collective topological mechanism.
method: Braids are treated within a locally free approximation, with the localization supported by analytical study of Brownian bridges on the asymptotic Cayley graph of a locally free group, complemented by numerical simulations.
result: For sufficiently long polymers the average transverse span approaches a finite limit, and a phase-transition-like crossover is conjectured: algebraic growth (with the usual square-root scaling) for few threads versus asymptotic localization for a large number of threads.
conclusion: Topologically induced localization arises purely from collective topological constraints, without quenched external disorder, and is conjectured to behave as a genuine phase transition in the number of threads.

title: Optical Angular Momentum And Pseudospin-orbit Coupling In Photonic Graphene
authors: Omri Bahat-Treidel, Daniel Leykam, Anton S. Desyatnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of structured laser beams carrying angular momentum (AM) as they undergo conical diffraction in photonic graphene. Using a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we demonstrate a surprising result: the beam's orbital AM tracks the dynamics of the lattice pseudospin rather than the AM of its slowly varying envelope. This finding provides evidence that pseudospin behaves as a genuine form of angular momentum. Furthermore, we explore beam propagation in staggered honeycomb lattices governed by the massive Dirac equation, revealing that the orbital AM is highly sensitive to both the band gap size and the envelope's initial AM. We explain our numerical results by drawing an analogy with the orbital magnetization of electrons.
tldr: The paper studies structured laser beams carrying angular momentum in photonic graphene and shows that orbital angular momentum tracks lattice pseudospin dynamics rather than the envelope angular momentum.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify whether pseudospin in photonic honeycomb lattices behaves as a genuine angular momentum and to understand angular-momentum dynamics in conical diffraction and massive Dirac settings.
method: They combine numerical simulations with analytical calculations of paraxial beam propagation in photonic graphene and staggered honeycomb lattices, drawing an analogy to orbital magnetization of electrons.
result: Orbital angular momentum is found to follow the lattice pseudospin dynamics, and in staggered honeycomb lattices it depends sensitively on the band gap and the initial envelope angular momentum.
conclusion: The work provides evidence that pseudospin can act as an effective angular momentum in photonic lattice systems and links structured-light propagation to massive Dirac physics.

title: The Galois Actions On Braided Fusion Categories
authors: Andrew Schopieray
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note harmonizes two classical topics: minimal modular extensions of braided fusion categories and the Galois action on modular fusion categories. Their common generalizations are Galois-modular extensions, which always exist when a braided fusion category [MATH] is pseudounitary. Each extension induces a Galois action on the simple objects of [MATH]. Up to integral equivalence, the Galois-modular extensions of [MATH] form a torsor over an explicit group of homomorphisms from [MATH] to the invertible objects of order dividing two in the symmetric center [MATH] of [MATH]. If [MATH] is Tannakian and [MATH] has a minimal modular extension, all minimal modular extensions induce one canonical Galois action. We prove that many facts about the modular data of modular fusion categories extend to pseudounitary premodular fusion categories as well via the Galois action.
tldr: The paper studies Galois-modular extensions of braided fusion categories and Galois actions on their simple objects, extending modular data results to pseudounitary premodular categories.
motivation: It aims to unify minimal modular extensions of braided fusion categories with the Galois action on modular fusion categories into a common framework.
method: The author introduces Galois-modular extensions, proves existence for pseudounitary braided fusion categories, and classifies such extensions up to integral equivalence as a torsor over homomorphisms into order-two invertible objects in the symmetric center.
result: For Tannakian categories with a minimal modular extension, all minimal modular extensions induce one canonical Galois action, and many modular-data facts extend to pseudounitary premodular fusion categories.
conclusion: The work provides a categorical algebraic framework for Galois actions on fusion categories, with relevance primarily to pure mathematics rather than quantum information theory as defined here.

title: Translate, Then Decide: Asymptotic Optimality Of Latent-space Control In Bistable Systems
authors: Arthur Castello B. de Oliveira
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper asks whether an optimal decision can be separated from the physical dynamics on which it acts. It studies this question through minimum-energy barrier crossing in scalar bistable systems. It characterizes the finite-horizon optimal feedback and shows that, as the horizon grows, it converges to a law that doubles and reverses the drift while it opposes crossing, and switches off once the barrier is passed. In physical coordinates, this law inherits the plant's nonlinearity, entangling decision and dynamics. We show that a plant-specific translation of state, input, and time maps every double well in the considered class to the same unit-rate linear world model, allowing a downstream decision stage to use a single plant-independent control primitive. This separation generally loses optimality at finite horizons because the translation does not preserve the physical control energy. Nevertheless, we prove that the excess physical energy of the layered controller vanishes as the horizon grows and that its limiting feedback reproduces the asymptotic optimum exactly. Thus, translation and optimization generally do not commute at a finite horizon, but commute in the asymptotic limit.
tldr: The paper studies whether optimal decision-making can be separated from physical dynamics in classical scalar bistable systems via a plant-specific translation to a unit-rate linear world model.
motivation: It asks whether an optimal control decision can be decoupled from the physical plant dynamics on which it acts, using minimum-energy barrier crossing as a testbed.
method: The authors characterize finite-horizon optimal feedback, construct a translation of state, input, and time mapping double-well systems to a common linear model, and analyze the energy loss of the resulting layered controller.
result: The translated controller is generally suboptimal at finite horizons because the translation does not preserve physical control energy, but its excess energy vanishes asymptotically and it reproduces the optimal limiting feedback.
conclusion: Translation and optimization do not commute at finite horizon, but they commute in the asymptotic limit, enabling a plant-independent control primitive for this class of bistable systems.

title: Functional Inequalities From The Fundamental Limits Of Bayesian Estimation
authors: Ilias Zadik Shuchen Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a Bayesian information-theoretic framework for proving functional inequalities for log-concave measures. Motivated by Klartag and Ordentlich, we establish a unified equivalence between [MATH]-Sobolev inequalities and Bayesian estimation lower bounds: for a large class of smooth convex [MATH], a log-concave measure [MATH] satisfies a [MATH]-Sobolev inequality with constant [MATH] if and only if for [MATH], any [MATH], and any real-valued measurable [MATH], the Bayes risk of estimating [MATH] under the [MATH]-Bregman loss from the Gaussian additive observation [MATH] is at least a [MATH]-fraction of that of the trivial estimator. Combining it with direct information-theoretic arguments, such as testing-to-estimation reductions, we obtain old and new functional inequalities: - For the Poincar\'e inequality, corresponding to [MATH], we give a simple static information-theoretic proof that the Poincar\'e constant of an isotropic log-concave measure on [MATH] is [MATH], first proven via stochastic localization in the seminal work of Lee and Vempala. - For the log-Sobolev inequality, corresponding to [MATH], we prove that all smooth [MATH]-subgaussian log-concave measures [MATH] satisfy [MATH], surpassing the recent state-of-the-art bound of [MATH] by Bizeul. In parallel and independent work, OpenAI claimed the optimal bound [MATH] in their October 6, 2026 release of 722 papers. - Finally, we give a Bayesian reformulation of the common structure of the three recent proofs of the Kannan--Lov\'asz--Simonovits conjecture, a dimension-free Poincar\'e bound for isotropic log-concave measures [BK26; BKL26; SZ26]. Tools from the study of the "low-degree MMSE" in computational complexity of statistical inference motivate and recast key steps and quantities of these proofs.
tldr: The paper develops a Bayesian information-theoretic framework connecting Sobolev-type functional inequalities for log-concave measures to lower bounds in Bayesian estimation.
motivation: The authors aim to unify and simplify proofs of functional inequalities such as Poincaré and log-Sobolev inequalities by relating them to Bayesian estimation lower bounds.
method: They establish an equivalence between Bregman-Sobolev inequalities and Bayes risk lower bounds under Gaussian additive observations, then apply information-theoretic reductions to derive old and new inequalities.
result: They recover a known Poincaré constant bound for isotropic log-concave measures, prove a new log-Sobolev bound for subgaussian log-concave measures, and reformulate recent proofs of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
conclusion: The framework provides a Bayesian perspective on functional inequalities and connects them to estimation-theoretic and computational-complexity tools, but it is purely classical and not quantum-related.

title: Exact Transport-Information Correspondence For Distribution-Adaptive Discretization
authors: Koretaka Yuge
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discretization of continuous probability distributions is an operation on the sample space, and the structure induced by this operation cannot generally be determined solely from information geometry. In our recent work on unavoidable canonical nonlinearity (UCN), we established a non-arbitrary connection between the transport cost associated with discretization and the information-geometric indistinguishability of continuous probability distributions. Through the transport-information correspondence, the UCN quantify the information-theoretic cost due to discretization as the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence between nearby continuous distributions associated with the discretization geometry. In the original UCN construction, discretization is implemented by transporting the probability mass within each cell to its geometric centroid. The resulting transport-information correspondence, however, is derived under specific conditions involving the cell geometry, spatial coverage, and the vanishing-cell-scale limit. In this work, we introduce an alternative local-map discretization scheme in which the probability mass within each cell is transported to its own probability-weighted centroid. This change in the representative-point selection enables an exact expression for the transport cost of each cell in terms of the covariance matrix of its conditional probability distribution and the Fisher metric of the underlying continuous family. We establish an exact correspondence between the resulting transport cost and the expectation of the associated Fisher-induced quadratic form, without requiring uniform cell geometry, complete coverage of the sample space, or an infinitesimal cell-scale limit. The proposed construction thus generalizes the transport-information correspondence to finite-scale discretization using arbitrary collections of non-overlapping bounded convex sets.
tldr: The paper derives an exact transport-information correspondence for distribution-adaptive discretization using local probability-weighted centroid maps.
motivation: Prior work established a transport-information correspondence for discretization only under restrictive assumptions such as uniform cell geometry, full coverage, and vanishing cell scale.
method: The authors introduce a local-map discretization scheme transporting mass within each cell to its probability-weighted centroid, then express the per-cell transport cost via the conditional covariance matrix and the Fisher metric.
result: They obtain an exact correspondence between transport cost and the expectation of a Fisher-induced quadratic form for arbitrary collections of non-overlapping bounded convex sets at finite scale.
conclusion: This generalizes the transport-information correspondence to finite-scale discretization without requiring uniform geometry, complete coverage, or infinitesimal cells.

title: Linear Maps Of $C^*$-algebras Preserving Norm Parallelism
authors: Chi-Kwong Li, Ming-Cheng Tsai, Ya-Shu Wang, Ngai-Ching Wong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two elements [MATH] in a normed space are parallel if [MATH] for some [MATH]; they form a triangle equality attaining (TEA) pair if [MATH]. For finite-dimensional complex [MATH]-algebras other than [MATH] and [MATH], bijective linear maps on these algebras preserving parallel or TEA pairs are scalar multiples of isometries. For unital abelian algebras with spectra containing at least three points, preservation in both directions gives the same conclusion. We obtain corresponding results for type I factors, simple type I [MATH]-algebras, and unitarily invariant operator spaces under additional continuity and finite-rank hypotheses. All results for [MATH] and [MATH] hold over both real and complex fields.
tldr: Characterizes bijective linear maps on finite-dimensional C*-algebras and related operator spaces that preserve norm-parallel or triangle-equality-attaining pairs, showing they are scalar multiples of isometries under stated hypotheses.
motivation: The work studies how geometric relations in normed spaces—specifically parallelism and triangle equality—constrain linear preservers on C*-algebras and type I factors.
method: The authors analyze bijective linear maps preserving parallel or TEA pairs on finite-dimensional complex C*-algebras, unital abelian algebras with sufficiently large spectra, type I factors, simple type I C*-algebras, and unitarily invariant operator spaces under continuity and finite-rank assumptions.
result: For finite-dimensional complex C*-algebras excluding certain small cases, such preservers are scalar multiples of isometries; analogous conclusions are obtained for the additional classes under extra hypotheses, with real-field versions for small algebras.
conclusion: Norm-parallelism and TEA-pair preservation impose strong isometric structure on linear maps of C*-algebras, extending preserver results across several operator-algebraic settings.

title: Local Information Processing Capacity: Anatomy Of Computation In Neuromorphic Systems
authors: Jiaxuan Chen, Daiki Nishioka, Yicheng Song, Ryo Iguchi, Sota Hikasa, Hina Kitano, Akira Hirose, Takashi Tsuchiya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many neuromorphic systems possess rich internal computational structures shaped by their physical dynamics. However, existing metrics characterize only global computation, leaving these local structures unresolved despite their importance for system interpretation, optimization and miniaturization. Here, we introduce local information processing capacity (L-IPC), which represents individual dynamical states as vectors in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and decomposes their computational properties through subspace projections onto nonlinearity orders and memory steps, with the residual quantifying computational irrelevance. Applied to three systems with comparable global capacities (an echo state network, an ion-gating reservoir and a spin-wave reservoir), L-IPC reveals markedly different distributions of computation, ranging from homogeneous to spatially, temporally and spectrally structured patterns. These local profiles further guide task-specific pruning, outperforming standard approaches at the same size in the structured systems. These results establish L-IPC as a general framework for anatomizing computation and guiding task-adaptive design in neuromorphic systems.
tldr: The authors introduce a local information processing capacity (L-IPC) metric that decomposes the computational capabilities of individual dynamical states in neuromorphic/reservoir systems into nonlinearity orders and memory steps.
motivation: Existing capacity metrics for neuromorphic systems capture only global computation and cannot resolve the rich internal structure shaped by physical dynamics, which limits interpretation, optimization, and miniaturization.
method: Each dynamical state is represented as a vector in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, and its computational properties are decomposed via subspace projections onto nonlinearity orders and memory steps, with the residual quantifying computational irrelevance; the metric is applied to an echo state network, an ion-gating reservoir, and a spin-wave reservoir.
result: Systems with comparable global capacity show markedly different local distributions of computation (homogeneous vs. spatially, temporally, and spectrally structured), and these local profiles enable task-specific pruning that outperforms standard pruning at equal system size.
conclusion: L-IPC provides a general framework for anatomizing computation and guiding task-adaptive design in neuromorphic hardware.

title: Rotated-Frame Determinant Discovery For Ground- And Excited-State Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction
authors: Yukihiro Okuno
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI) constructs a variational determinant space from measurements of a prepared electronic state, but finite-shot sampling can repeatedly observe high-probability determinants, limiting efficient discovery of configurations important for an accurate selected-CI description. We introduce rotate--sample--unrotate (RSU) determinant discovery, in which the same state is sampled in complementary orbital frames and the observed rotated determinants generate a finite set of candidates in the canonical basis. The Hamiltonian is then diagonalized in an orthonormal selected-CI space without enumerating the full determinant space. State-targeted orbital frames are constructed from an initial selected-CI wavefunction and its external residual. For excited states, we combine RSU with the generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) to prepare target-specific sampling states. Candidate GQE circuits are evaluated by classical selected-CI diagonalization in finite sampled spaces, so the quantum procedure requires only state preparation and determinant sampling. For N[MATH], exact-state controls isolate the determinant-discovery effect: at the stretched geometry, residual-natural-orbital RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots, compared with 20,000 shots for conventional QSCI. The improvement persists with approximate GQE-prepared states and is also observed for target excited states. These results demonstrate improved finite-shot determinant discovery in QSCI for both ground and excited states.
tldr: The paper introduces a rotated-frame sampling strategy to improve determinant discovery in quantum selected configuration interaction for ground- and excited-state electronic structure calculations.
motivation: Finite-shot sampling in QSCI tends to repeatedly observe high-probability determinants, hindering efficient discovery of configurations needed for accurate selected-CI descriptions.
method: The rotate-sample-unrotate approach samples the same electronic state in complementary orbital frames, generates candidate determinants in the canonical basis, and diagonalizes the Hamiltonian in an orthonormal selected-CI space; excited states use GQE-prepared sampling states.
result: For N2, residual-natural-orbital RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots versus 20,000 shots for conventional QSCI, and the improvement persists with approximate GQE states and for excited states.
conclusion: RSU improves finite-shot determinant discovery in QSCI for both ground and excited states, but the work is specialized to quantum chemistry and does not address the user's quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems interests.

title: A Closed-form Design Rule For Photonic Hopfions Of Arbitrary Order
authors: Ali Nadarloo, Mohammad Javad Hajiahmadi, Mohammad Soleimani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological textures of light are robust against perturbation and are emerging as carriers of information and probes of light-matter interaction. The most intricate of them, the photonic hopfion, in which the loops of different polarization states are linked, has so far been assembled from chosen superpositions of laser modes, with weights set by hand or found by numerical optimization. Here we replace this search with a design rule. Two scalar beams, an optical vortex of order [MATH] and a field with n dark rings, propagate in closed form, and their phases on one plane are the two masks of a metasurface that controls two orthogonal polarizations. Although a beam, unlike the closed spaces of topology, extends to infinity, we prove that it is a hopfion of order [MATH] whenever three algebraic conditions on the ring coefficients and the vortex order hold, and that the polarization loops of every state that the far field does not reach then link exactly [MATH] times; each condition guards against one way in which the topology can escape. The order is thus chosen on paper and the device follows directly, without optimization. In scalar simulation, one terahertz metasurface geometry produces hopfions up to order nine, and a full-wave simulation of the complete first-order device preserves its topology. The rule applies to any platform that shapes the phases of two orthogonal polarizations.
tldr: The paper presents a closed-form design rule for generating photonic hopfions of arbitrary order using metasurface phase masks and two scalar beams.
motivation: Photonic hopfions are topologically robust optical textures useful for information carrying and light-matter interaction, but their construction has required hand-tuned or numerically optimized mode superpositions.
method: Two scalar beams—an optical vortex and a field with dark rings—are propagated in closed form, and their phases on one plane define metasurface masks for two orthogonal polarizations; algebraic conditions on ring coefficients and vortex order guarantee hopfion topology.
result: The design rule yields hopfions up to order nine in scalar simulation with a terahertz metasurface geometry, and a full-wave simulation of a first-order device preserves the topology.
conclusion: The approach replaces numerical optimization with a direct design rule applicable to any platform that shapes two orthogonal polarization phases, enabling on-demand photonic hopfion generation.

title: When Light Travels With Infinite Speed: The Electromagnetic Loop Circuits
authors: Pierre Seppecher Graeme W Milton
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Considering the ideal limit where the speed of light is infinite, or more precisely where the permittivity and permeability of the vaccuum are both zero, we construct a new type of electromagnetic circuit that we name an EM-loop circuit. These consist of wires having very high permittivity (E-wires) and wires having very high permeability (M-wires). These are threaded together by coils, the E-wire loops and M-wire loops. Some of the loops are terminal loops, pierced by an applied magnetic flux (for E-wire loops) or an applied displacement field (for M-wire loops) that are outside the vacuum since it does not support these fields. The response is the net flux of displacement field through a cross section of each E-wire terminal loop and the net magnetic flux through a cross section of each terminal M-wire loop. To calculate this response, the fields at the internal loops (those that are not terminal loops) are eliminated from the equations.It turns out that the response is governed by a new class of function pairs - dual Herglotz functions. Superpositions of a special class of EM-loop circuits, termed fundamental, allow us to realize any pair of dual Herglotz functions. Thus, we have obtained a complete characterization of the response functions of EM-loop circuits.
tldr: The authors construct a new class of electromagnetic 'EM-loop circuits' in the idealized limit of infinite speed of light (zero vacuum permittivity and permeability) and completely characterize their response functions via a new class of dual Herglotz functions.
motivation: The paper explores the mathematical and physical consequences of the idealized limit where vacuum permittivity and permeability vanish, aiming to define a novel circuit paradigm built from high-permittivity and high-permeability wires threaded into loops.
method: E-wires and M-wires are threaded together into internal and terminal loops; terminal loops are pierced by externally applied magnetic flux or displacement field, and internal-loop fields are eliminated from the governing equations to derive the input-output response.
result: The response is shown to be governed by pairs of 'dual Herglotz functions', and superpositions of fundamental EM-loop circuits are proven sufficient to realize any such dual Herglotz function pair, yielding a complete characterization.
conclusion: EM-loop circuits provide a fully characterized new circuit class in the infinite-light-speed limit, with mathematical structure analogous to network synthesis but entirely classical-electromagnetic in nature.

title: The Two-loop Lamb Shift: The Final Missing Contribution
authors: J. Sommerfeldt, V. A. Yerokhin, Z. Harman, C. H. Keitel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The last significant unknown contribution to the two-loop Lamb shift, namely the electron self-energy with vacuum-polarization insertion into the photon line, is determined including higher-order effects in the parameter [MATH], with [MATH] being the fine-structure constant and [MATH] the nuclear charge number. Our calculation improves the accuracy of theoretical predictions for energy levels and transition energies in heavy hydrogen-like and lithium-like ions by up to one order of magnitude, enabling more stringent comparisons between theory and available experimental results. These results pave the way for more precise tests of quantum electrodynamics in the strong-field regime, as well as for accurate determinations of nuclear charge radii.
tldr: This paper computes the last unknown two-loop Lamb-shift contribution—the electron self-energy with a vacuum-polarization insertion in the photon line—including higher-order terms in alpha*Z for heavy hydrogen-like and lithium-like ions.
motivation: The two-loop Lamb shift contained one remaining uncalculated contribution that limited the precision of bound-state QED predictions for heavy few-electron ions.
method: Analytical and numerical evaluation of the two-loop self-energy diagrams with vacuum-polarization insertions, expanded to higher orders in the parameter alpha*Z.
result: Theoretical energy levels and transition energies in heavy hydrogen-like and lithium-like ions are improved in accuracy by up to one order of magnitude, enabling tighter theory-experiment comparisons.
conclusion: The results enable more precise tests of QED in the strong-field regime and more accurate determinations of nuclear charge radii.

title: Conditions For Normality Of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle In The Absence Of State Constraints
authors: Andr\'e Tits, Pierre-Antoine Absil, No\'e Tits
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is said to be "normal" for the problem at hand when it has a solution (maximizer u*) that explicitly involves the problem's cost function, making the maximum principle helpful (while in the opposite situation it is of no help). The aim of the present paper is, for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, to identify classes of problems for which the Principle is normal. General conditions are introduced that guarantee normality, and classes of problems that satisfy these conditions are identified. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the control values) "augmented" reachable set, with cost along an upward vertical axis, has a convex lower-boundary function and the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the reachable state set, with the terminal constraint within the affine hull of that set. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the values of the control signal) "augmented" (with the cost value along an upward "vertical axis") reachable set has a "convex" lower boundary for which the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the set of reachable states. Special attention is given to Lagrange steering problems: sufficient conditions are obtained on a nested sequence of sub-classes of such problems, culminating with the class of steering problems with scalar control signal and linear time-invariant (LTI) state dynamics and objective integrand, for which normality is guaranteed whenever all eigenvalues of the state dynamics matrix A are real (e.g., if A is symmetric or triangular or the system is overdamped) or have small enough imaginary parts; simple 2 x 2 examples show that, in contrast with the situation in the finite-dimensional case, this property does not extend to arbitrary A matrices.
tldr: The paper derives general sufficient conditions guaranteeing that Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is 'normal' for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, including a detailed treatment of steering problems.
motivation: When the maximum principle is abnormal, its multiplier conditions carry no information about the cost, making it useless in practice; the authors therefore seek structural conditions under which normality is assured.
method: The authors introduce general conditions on the augmented reachable set (control-bounded, cost along a vertical axis) — such as a convex lower-boundary function and optimal terminal state in the relative interior — and identify problem classes satisfying them, specializing to Lagrange steering problems with scalar control and LTI dynamics.
result: Normality is guaranteed for nested sub-classes culminating in scalar-control LTI steering problems where all eigenvalues of A are real or have sufficiently small imaginary parts, with 2x2 counterexamples showing this does not extend to arbitrary A.
conclusion: The work provides checkable geometric and spectral criteria for normality of the maximum principle, though analogies with the finite-dimensional case fail for general dynamics matrices.

title: Hotplug Coded Caching: Embedding The Yma And Interference Elimination Schemes Via Reed--Muller Codes
authors: Daniela Tuninetti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the hotplug coded caching model, [MATH] users fill their caches of size [MATH] as a function of [MATH] files, but only an unknown subset of [MATH] users is active in the delivery phase. We recently showed that (i) under uncoded placement, offline users cause a strict load penalty at intermediate memory sizes, so that coded placement is needed; and (ii) for [MATH], every classical scheme with row-wise placement, including the scheme of Gomez-Vilardebo (GV), can be embedded in a Reed-Solomon code, which removes the penalty. In this note, we show that every point of the scheme of Yu, Maddah-Ali and Avestimehr (YMA) for a classical system with [MATH] users is achievable in the hotplug model for every [MATH]. Each user is associated with a hyperplane and each file with a homogeneous polynomial; each user caches the restriction of the polynomial to its hyperplane, and the subfiles seen by the active users are the values of the polynomial at the points where their hyperplanes meet. This is a projective Reed-Muller code, which reduces to the Reed-Solomon code when each subfile is cached by one user. We then show, by an existence argument, that every classical scheme whose cache is a linear compression of the Maddah-Ali-Niesen cache and whose correctness holds for generic coefficients can also be embedded over a sufficiently large field; this includes the interference elimination (IE) schemes of Tian and Chen. These embeddings complement the Reed-Solomon one, which allows any row-wise placement and any delivery. Together with past work, our results show that every point attained by a GV, YMA or IE scheme ([MATH] for IE), and every corner point of the linear tradeoff for [MATH], is achievable in the hotplug model with a load that does not depend on [MATH]. Whether the optimal hotplug tradeoff depends only on [MATH] remains open, but these results support a positive answer.
tldr: The paper shows that classical YMA and interference-elimination coded caching schemes can be embedded into the hotplug caching model via projective Reed-Muller codes, achieving loads independent of the number of active users.
motivation: In hotplug coded caching, offline (inactive) users incur a load penalty at intermediate memory sizes under uncoded placement, motivating coded placement schemes that remove this penalty.
method: Each user is associated with a hyperplane and each file with a homogeneous polynomial; users cache restrictions of the polynomial to their hyperplane, and active users recover subfiles from values at hyperplane intersections, yielding a projective Reed-Muller code construction, complemented by an existence argument for linear-compression schemes.
result: Every point of the YMA scheme and every IE scheme (for M>=3) is achievable in the hotplug model with load independent of the number of active users, matching classical tradeoff corner points.
conclusion: The embeddings support the conjecture that the optimal hotplug tradeoff depends only on the total number of users, though this remains open.

title: Bmv Conjecture And Positivity Of Spectral Shift For Relatively Schatten Perturbations
authors: Anna Skripka Chandan Pradhan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish BMV-type results and prove the positivity-preserving property and uniqueness of support-normalized spectral shift functions of arbitrary order for semibounded operators with relatively Schatten-von Neumann perturbations. We also derive correlation inequalities in the relative Hilbert-Schmidt case. These results build on a new positivity-preserving property for the trace of a higher-order operator derivative along a relatively Schatten direction and are obtained using methods of multilinear operator integration and approximation.
tldr: The paper establishes BMV-type results and proves positivity and uniqueness of support-normalized spectral shift functions of arbitrary order for semibounded operators under relatively Schatten-von Neumann perturbations.
motivation: Spectral shift functions are central objects in perturbation theory and trace formulas, and the Bessis-Moussa-Villani (BMV) conjecture concerns positivity of traces of polynomial operator expressions; the authors aim to extend positivity-preserving properties to higher-order spectral shift functions under relative Schatten perturbations.
method: The results are obtained via multilinear operator integration and approximation techniques, building on a newly established positivity-preserving property for the trace of a higher-order operator derivative along a relatively Schatten direction.
result: They prove the positivity-preserving property and uniqueness of support-normalized spectral shift functions of arbitrary order, derive BMV-type results, and obtain correlation inequalities in the relative Hilbert-Schmidt case.
conclusion: The work extends the scope of BMV-type positivity results and spectral shift theory to higher orders and relatively Schatten perturbations, providing new operator-theoretic inequalities of potential use in mathematical physics.

title: Magnetic Bloch Eigenvalue Problems In Nonuniform Periodic Magnetic Fields: A Fourier-finite Difference Approach
authors: Yuanwei Lai Xueyang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study magnetic Bloch eigenvalue problems for two-dimensional magnetic Schr\"odinger operators with nonuniform periodic magnetic fields and periodic scalar potentials, and develop a hybrid Fourier-finite difference discretization. A Landau-type gauge is constructed by solving a periodic Poisson equation. Under the integer magnetic flux condition, the magnetic Bloch boundary conditions are incorporated through shifts of Fourier-mode indices. The method combines link-variable-based covariant central differences in the [MATH]-direction with a Fourier pseudospectral discretization in the [MATH]-direction, yielding a Hermitian discrete Hamiltonian. The resulting eigenvalue problems are solved using a LOBPCG method. Under appropriate regularity assumptions, we establish a fully discrete consistency residual estimate of order [MATH]. With suitable spectral separation and eigenspace dimension-preserving conditions, error estimates of the same order are derived for isolated eigenvalues and their associated eigenspaces. Numerical experiments show second-order convergence in the finite difference direction and rapid error reduction with increasing Fourier resolution, and illustrate band degeneracies and eigenstate distributions in nonuniform periodic magnetic fields.
tldr: The paper develops a hybrid Fourier-finite difference numerical method for magnetic Bloch eigenvalue problems with nonuniform periodic magnetic fields.
motivation: Magnetic Bloch eigenvalue problems are important for understanding quantum particles in periodic magnetic fields, but efficient accurate discretizations for nonuniform fields remain challenging.
method: The authors construct a Landau-type gauge via a periodic Poisson equation and combine link-variable covariant finite differences in one direction with Fourier pseudospectral discretization in the other, solving the resulting Hermitian eigenvalue problem with LOBPCG.
result: They prove consistency and eigenvalue/eigenspace error estimates under regularity and spectral separation assumptions, and numerically demonstrate second-order convergence in the finite-difference direction and rapid Fourier-resolution convergence.
conclusion: The hybrid scheme provides an effective numerical approach for magnetic Bloch problems, but the work is a numerical analysis contribution rather than one aligned with quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Ray-Tracing-Based Dynamic Channel Sounding With Autoregressive Wi-Fi Csi Prediction
authors: Lyutianyang Zhang, Yixin Ying, Liu Cao, Vanlin Sathya, Jinke Ren, Shuguang Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Channel sounding in Wi-Fi multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems must balance channel state information (CSI) accuracy against CSI acquisition overhead. Device mobility causes channel aging, while autoregressive CSI prediction introduces errors that accumulate over sounding intervals. However, standardized statistical channel models cannot fully capture the environment-specific channel dynamics encountered in physical artificial intelligence (AI) applications, motivating the use of Sionna-based ray tracing to evaluate CSI prediction under device mobility and evolving propagation geometry. This paper develops a dynamic sounding framework that integrates autoregressive CSI prediction with signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR)-constrained interval selection. A Transformer with rotary position embedding that converts device positions into CSI sequences predicts CSI across multiple subcarriers for beamforming updates between sounding exchanges. We formulate sounding-interval selection as a predicted average-throughput maximization problem under per-stream SINR lower-bound constraints, including CSI acquisition and processing overhead. A prediction-error perturbation analysis provides the SINR bounds, and cumulative-sum enumeration globally solves the finite single-variable problem. Actual SINR feasibility holds whenever the prediction errors satisfy the bounds. Ray-tracing experiments assess channel prediction, trajectory transfer, and autoregressive prediction errors. In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3%, 112.7%, and 119.1% over stale CSI for linear, circular, and cosine trajectories, respectively.
tldr: The paper develops a ray-tracing-based dynamic Wi-Fi channel sounding framework that uses a Transformer with rotary position embeddings to autoregressively predict CSI and selects sounding intervals via SINR-constrained throughput maximization.
motivation: Wi-Fi MIMO channel sounding must trade CSI accuracy against acquisition overhead, and device mobility causes channel aging while autoregressive prediction compounds errors; standardized statistical models fail to capture environment-specific dynamics.
method: Sionna-based ray tracing is combined with a Transformer (rotary position embedding) that maps device positions to multi-subcarrier CSI sequences, plus a predicted-average-throughput maximization for sounding-interval selection solved by cumulative-sum enumeration with prediction-error perturbation bounds on SINR.
result: Ray-tracing experiments evaluate channel prediction, trajectory transfer, and error accumulation; in Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3%, 112.7%, and 119.1% over stale CSI for linear, circular, and cosine trajectories.
conclusion: Autoregressive CSI prediction with SINR-aware interval selection substantially mitigates channel aging in mobile Wi-Fi MIMO systems, though the work is purely classical wireless engineering with no quantum information, thermodynamic, or quantum-network content.

title: Toward Shifted Symplectic Chiralization: Deformation Of Courant Algebroids
authors: Noriaki Ikeda Wenda Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the chiralization of Poisson--Lie theory through graded symplectic geometry. We compare Courant deformations and classical [MATH]- and [MATH]-matrix constructions, obtaining integrable hierarchies and free field realizations. We give a variational description of the obstruction to Lie conformal bialgebra compatibility and recover Liberati's obstruction in the Virasoro case. We also introduce a vertex bialgebra analogue of quantized universal enveloping algebras and construct explicit quantizations to all orders of Cartan type Lie conformal bialgebra structures on [MATH]. These results contribute to the first author's broader programme of developing shifted symplectic chiralization as a geometric method for constructing chiral analogues of Poisson-Lie structures via [MATH]-shifted symplectic geometry, and exploring its connections with AKSZ theory and quantization.
tldr: The paper develops a shifted symplectic geometry approach to chiralization of Poisson–Lie theory, Courant algebroids, and Lie conformal bialgebras.
motivation: The authors aim to extend Poisson–Lie structures to chiral/vertex algebraic settings using graded symplectic geometry and to connect this with AKSZ theory and quantization.
method: They compare Courant deformations with classical r-matrix constructions, derive integrable hierarchies and free-field realizations, and use variational obstructions to Lie conformal bialgebra compatibility.
result: They recover Liberati's obstruction in the Virasoro case, introduce a vertex bialgebra analogue of quantized universal enveloping algebras, and construct all-order quantizations of Cartan-type Lie conformal bialgebra structures.
conclusion: The work contributes to a broader programme of shifted symplectic chiralization as a geometric method for constructing chiral analogues of Poisson–Lie structures.

title: The Cnf Encoding Complexity Of Boolean Functions
authors: Andrew Krapivin, Benjamin Przybocki, Bernardo Subercaseaux
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the minimum number of clauses required to encode a boolean function into a CNF formula with auxiliary variables. Our main result is that if a boolean function can be evaluated in nondeterministic time [MATH] (in the RAM model) with [MATH] bits of advice such that at most [MATH] bits of advice are accessed for each input, then it admits a CNF encoding with [MATH] clauses. This constitutes a nonuniform generalization of Robson's (TCS'91) variant of the Cook--Levin theorem, for which a na\"ive generalization would yield [MATH] clauses; our applications leverage [MATH] to obtain significantly better bounds. Since preprocessed data structures can be modeled as computation with advice, our result allows us to translate space- and time-efficient data structures to compact CNF encodings. As an application, we derandomize a data structure of Larsen and Williams (SODA'17) to show that every [MATH]-CNF function on [MATH] inputs can be encoded with [MATH] clauses. Notably, despite encoding a [MATH]-CNF function, the encoding itself necessarily contains clauses of unbounded width, since an information-theoretic argument shows that the minimum number of bounded-width clauses to encode such functions is [MATH] in the worst case. In general terms, our results imply that for a wide variety of NP-complete problems, one can reduce to CNF-SAT in a way that results in asymptotically fewer clauses than previously known methods.
tldr: The paper bounds the minimum number of clauses needed to encode Boolean functions as CNF formulas with auxiliary variables, deriving compact encodings from nondeterministic time-and-advice computations.
motivation: Preprocessing and data-structure lower/upper bounds can be translated into CNF encoding size, so tighter encodings are desirable for SAT-based reductions of NP-complete problems.
method: A nonuniform generalization of Robson's variant of the Cook–Levin theorem is proved: functions evaluable in nondeterministic RAM time with limited advice admit CNF encodings with few clauses, exploiting advice to beat naive bounds.
result: Every k-CNF function on n inputs can be encoded with asymptotically fewer clauses than before (derandomizing a Larsen–Williams data structure), though the encoding necessarily uses unbounded-width clauses, as an information-theoretic argument shows bounded-width encodings require exponentially many clauses.
conclusion: For many NP-complete problems, reductions to CNF-SAT can use asymptotically fewer clauses than previous methods, though the work is purely classical complexity theory with no quantum information or thermodynamic content.

title: Private Vulnerability Testing For User Oversharing
authors: Alexander Boyd, Daniel Gardham, Nishanth Sastry, Suparna de
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users can inadvertently increase their vulnerability to privacy attacks by oversharing personal information. In particular, the combination of individually innocuous attributes can place a user in a sufficiently small population to enable linkage or re-identification attacks. We present a privacy-preserving mechanism that allows users to determine whether the information they disclose places them below a predefined population threshold, without revealing their query or the data of other users. Our setting presents several practical challenges: users contributing data may be offline when queries are made, queries may select arbitrary subsets of attributes, and neither server should learn the queried population or its size. We address these challenges using secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation. Our protocol provides computational privacy against a malicious client and semi-honest, non-colluding servers, while supporting arbitrary queries and dynamic database updates. We define reactive [MATH]-privacy for a dynamically evolving database and prove that our construction satisfies it, with the sequence of permitted threshold outputs defining the information available to the adversary across an execution. We optimise the protocol using oblivious-transfer extensions and pre-computation, achieving sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets of up to one million records.
tldr: The paper designs a privacy-preserving protocol that lets users check whether their disclosed attributes put them below a population-size threshold, without revealing queries or other users' data.
motivation: Individually innocuous attributes can combine to make a user re-identifiable, so users need a way to test their own oversharing risk without exposing personal data to servers or other users.
method: The protocol uses secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation across two semi-honest non-colluding servers, with oblivious-transfer extensions and precomputation for efficiency, and defines reactive privacy for a dynamically evolving database.
result: The construction is proven to satisfy the defined reactive privacy notion against a malicious client and semi-honest servers while supporting arbitrary attribute-subset queries and dynamic updates, with sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets up to one million records.
conclusion: The work provides a practical cryptographic tool for user-side privacy risk assessment, but it lies entirely in classical secure computation and is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Towards The Query Complexity Of Sampling Under Strong Log-Concavity And Log-Sobolev Inequalities
authors: Taiji Suzuki Huanjian Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the query complexity of sampling from smooth distributions on [MATH] using first-order oracles. For [MATH]-dimensional strongly log-concave targets with condition number [MATH], we prove that any randomized sampler requires [MATH] queries even from a constant warm start. This rules out polylogarithmic dimension dependence and strictly separates strongly log-concave sampling from Gaussian sampling. For targets with [MATH]-smooth potentials satisfying an [MATH]-log-Sobolev inequality with [MATH], we prove an [MATH] query lower bound for [MATH]. This shows that log-Sobolev sampling is strictly harder than strongly log-concave sampling. Our proofs construct instance-dependent tests that target samples typically pass but outputs of algorithms making few queries typically fail. For strongly log-concave targets, we embed a sequence of hidden Gaussian into high-degree tensor polynomial with smooth gates, forcing any algorithm to uncover the layers sequentially. The log-Sobolev construction hides a constant fraction of the target mass in angular caps while controlling the log-Sobolev constant via delicate estimates.
tldr: The paper establishes query-complexity lower bounds for sampling from smooth, strongly log-concave and log-Sobolev distributions using first-order oracles.
motivation: Understanding the intrinsic query cost of sampling is fundamental to algorithm design, and prior work left open whether polylogarithmic dimension dependence is achievable for strongly log-concave targets.
method: The authors construct adversarial instance-dependent tests: for strongly log-concave targets they embed nested hidden Gaussians into high-degree tensor polynomials with smooth gates, and for LSI targets they hide mass in angular caps while carefully bounding the log-Sobolev constant.
result: They prove a polynomial query lower bound even from a constant warm start for strongly log-concave targets, strictly separating them from Gaussian sampling, and an additional higher bound for LSI targets, showing LSI sampling is strictly harder.
conclusion: Strongly log-concave and log-Sobolev sampling have provably polynomial query complexity in dimension, ruling out polylogarithmic dependence and clarifying the hierarchy of sampling hardness.

title: AI-Assisted Classification Under Correlation Neglect And Trust
authors: Dingwen Kong, Liang Lyu, Saurabh Amin, Amine Bennouna, Daniel Huttenlocher, Asuman Ozdaglar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.
tldr: A behavioral model of human-AI collaborative binary decision-making that quantifies how correlation neglect and miscalibrated trust determine whether AI advice helps or harms accuracy.
motivation: AI assistants are increasingly used in decision pipelines, but it is unclear when a more accurate AI actually improves human accuracy, since overlapping evidence and human trust heuristics can offset or invert the benefit.
method: The authors build a closed-form Bayesian-style model with two behavioral primitives — awareness of evidence overlap (correlation neglect) and trust in the AI — yielding a phase diagram in AI capability and overlap space (complementarity, impairment, automation), then empirically identify the parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs (ChatBench, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8b).
result: The analysis shows correlation neglect can make workers less accurate with a more capable AI, undertrust can partially compensate, and the accuracy-optimal trust level depends on deployment parameters; empirically AI assistance gains 21 points but workers apply only ~25% of the Bayes-rational AI weight, with GPT-4o in the automation region and calibration recovering 2.6 points.
conclusion: Designing beneficial AI assistance requires jointly optimizing AI-side evidence independence and human-side trust calibration, not just improving raw AI accuracy.

title: The Complexity Of Unpredictability
authors: Dani Dorfman Aryan Agarwala
abstract: ArXiv:2611.05956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We initiate the study of middle-bit predictors: functions that take as input a string with one missing bit and try to predict that bit. These are closely related to next-bit predictors, a classical object in pseudorandomness. We study the deterministic complexity of computing an unpredictable distribution (UNPRED). Given a list of middle-bit predictors in circuit form and a parameter [MATH], output a multiset of strings such that each predictor succeeds with probability less than [MATH] on a uniformly sampled string from the multiset. We write [MATH] for the restriction to [MATH] predictors. We show that UNPRED offers a unified route towards resolving several major open problems in catalytic computation, the biggest of which is whether deterministic polynomial time (P and FP) can simulate catalytic logspace (CL and SearchCL). It is believed that [MATH]. We prove $[MATH][MATH]^1[MATH]^{^1}[MATH]^1[MATH]^1$ circuits in this way to solve a natural problem, thus advancing our understanding of Boolean circuits. Together, our results provide strong evidence that middle-bit predictors could be the key to unlocking several major open problems in catalytic computation, pseudorandomness, and Boolean circuit complexity.
tldr: The paper initiates the study of middle-bit predictors and defines the UNPRED problem to connect catalytic computation, pseudorandomness, and Boolean circuit complexity.
motivation: It aims to provide a unified complexity-theoretic route toward resolving major open problems, especially whether deterministic polynomial time can simulate catalytic logspace.
method: The authors introduce middle-bit predictors, formulate the deterministic complexity problem UNPRED over circuit-form predictors, and analyze its connections to catalytic computation and circuit lower bounds.
result: They show that UNPRED offers a unified approach to several open problems and use it to advance understanding of Boolean circuits via new circuit constructions.
conclusion: Middle-bit predictors are proposed as a potentially key concept for progress on open problems in catalytic computation, pseudorandomness, and Boolean circuit complexity.

title: Reconciling Privacy With Provenance For Language Model Watermarks
authors: Tatsunori Hashimoto Elise L. Han
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Watermarking has great potential for regulating the use of language models (LMs), but its deployment has been marred by controversy, as many users argue that fine-grained tracking of LM usage violates their privacy. This tension reduces the effectiveness of watermarks, as users engage in evasion strategies such as paraphrasing that can remove much of the watermark signal. We show that provenance and privacy can be reconciled if we shift the goal of watermark design from tracking individuals to estimating aggregate usage. We develop locally differentially private watermarks which provably limit the evidence that any individual text can contribute to detection, while still enabling accurate estimation of population frequencies. We introduce the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, a private and computationally efficient watermark that achieves accurate frequency estimation at high privacy levels across various models, sample sizes and generation entropies in settings that reflect realistic deployment scenarios. On C4 language modeling tasks, we attain [MATH] MSE with [MATH] mean absolute bias at a low [MATH] of 1, while in more challenging settings such as an essay writing task with only 100 text samples, we still find errors on the order of [MATH] MSE with [MATH] mean absolute bias at [MATH].
tldr: The paper introduces locally differentially private language-model watermarks, notably the Red-Green Sequence (RGS) watermark, that replace individual-level tracking with aggregate usage-frequency estimation.
motivation: Watermarking LMs for provenance raises privacy objections from users, who respond with evasion such as paraphrasing that destroys the watermark signal; the authors argue this tension can be resolved by reframing watermarking as population-level usage estimation rather than individual tracking.
method: They formalize locally differentially private watermarking that provably bounds the evidence any single text contributes to detection, and design the Red-Green Sequence watermark, a computationally efficient scheme for accurate frequency estimation under strong privacy constraints.
result: On C4 language modeling tasks the RGS watermark achieves low MSE and mean absolute bias at a privacy level of epsilon = 1, and remains accurate (errors on the order of small MSE/bias) in a demanding essay-writing setting with only 100 samples.
conclusion: Privacy and provenance can be reconciled by shifting watermark design goals to aggregate estimation, yielding practical, private, and efficient watermarking for realistic LM deployment.

title: Clear Human Web: Where A Person Vouches For Every Client
authors: Lorenzo Porcelli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.06286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary. The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.
tldr: The paper proposes a privacy-preserving web access model in which anonymous blind-signed personhood tokens, issued once per person, are spent to prove humanness without adding identity attributes.
motivation: The web cannot reliably distinguish human users from automated agents; network-address checks and CAPTCHA puzzles have been defeated by automated traffic, paid solving, and AI agents.
method: A person presents person identification data to a single issuer, receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, and the browser spends one token per participating site; in the optimum case a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession plus a per-site pseudonym replaces tokens.
result: The construction is formalized through five properties and seven adversaries, with a bound of k identities per person per site per epoch, reducing to k = 1 under a one-pseudonym-per-issuer constraint.
